articles.title_orig: China Presses Forward on Human Moon Landing Before 2030
articles.title_zh: China Presses Forward on Human Moon Landing Before 2030
articles.content_orig:
Image credit: CCTV/Inside Outer Space screengrab
China continues to chart its first crewed Moon landing before 2030, detailing current plans last weekend during the Seventh Manned Space Symposium in Beijing.
The two-day symposium drew more than 800 experts and scholars to explore how digital and intelligent technologies can advance human spaceflight.
Uncrewed test flights of the Mengzhou crewed spacecraft and the Lanyue lunar lander are planned ahead of a crewed Moon landing mission.
Wang Xiang, deputy chief designer of China’s manned space program, said a trio of astronauts will carry out the Moon mission, with two individuals landing on the lunar surface.
Image credit: CCTV/Inside Outer Space screengrab
“We will use the unmanned Lanyue lunar lander to verify all the key technologies throughout the entire crewed process as much as possible – including launch, entering the lunar orbit, rendezvous and docking with the Mengzhou spacecraft, landing and staying on the lunar surface, taking off again and re-docking with the crewed spaceship Mengzhou, so as to make sure the crewed flight will be safe and reliable,” Wang told China Central Television (CCTV).
Two Long March-10 carrier rockets will launch the Lanyue lunar lander and the Mengzhou spaceship in succession, then the two will conduct a rendezvous and docking in lunar orbit.
The Mengzhou can carry three astronauts between Earth and lunar orbit, with two of them riding the Lanyue lunar lander between lunar orbit and the lunar surface.
China’s Moon landing initiative will carry out, as planned, the Long March-10 carrier rocket technology verification flight, the first flights of the Mengzhou spaceship and the Lanyue lunar lander, and important missions such as the robotic Chang’e-7 lunar lander.
“When planning, we follow two principles,” Wang told CCTV . “First, for any task to be performed in lunar orbit, we will utilize the space station to conduct validation in near-Earth orbit whenever possible; second, for any crewed mission, we will try to fly it in an unmanned state first.”
To be utilized is the near-Earth version of the Long March-10 rocket to launch the near-Earth version of the Mengzhou spacecraft to perform space station missions in near-Earth orbit, added Wang, to validate the rocket’s basic technologies and the critical re-entry and return phases of the spacecraft.
“Then, we will use the lunar version of the Long March-10 rocket to launch the lunar version of the Mengzhou spacecraft to execute the lunar landing mission. This is a validation process for the rocket: near-Earth first, then the Moon,” said Wang.
Lanyue lunar lander. Image credit: CCTV/Inside Outer Space screengrab
The uncrewed flight mission of the Lanyue lander will allow for on-site collection of critical environmental data, including first-hand measured information on lunar surface temperature, lunar dust conditions, and the in-orbit performance of the spacecraft.
Wang said that the uncrewed flight mission of the Lanyue lander is also soliciting secondary payloads nationwide.
For a single mission, the total mass of the carried payloads will not exceed 50 kilograms, and the total power consumption will not exceed 100 watts.
“Because it is an unmanned mission, we will have some surplus resources, and we must make full use of them. Through a selection process, we will choose scientific experiment projects that are meaningful and necessary to be conducted on the Moon,” said Wang. “It is like giving them a ‘free ride’ to the Moon to conduct corresponding scientific experiments or technical explorations, achieving the goal of benefiting multiple parties with a single flight,” said Wang.

articles.title_orig: Stocks jump as oil prices tumble before midterms, tech shares rebound: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stocks jump as oil prices tumble before midterms, tech shares rebound: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Crude oil prices fell sharply Monday as senior U.S. and Iranian officials signal they are open to a diplomatic solution to the conflict that has disrupted energy markets for eight months.
Brent crude futures, the international benchmark, fell 6.4% to $106.20 a barrel as of 9:50 a.m. ET. U.S. West Texas Intermediate declined 6.5% to $97.35 per barrel.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump prefers not to use military force against Iran and would like to resolve the conflict diplomatically.
Trump has previously said that he will not attack Iran before the U.S. midterms. But the oil market had priced in the risk of a major military escalation after the elections.
The president "hasn't made a decision," Rubio told reporters over the weekend.
"What the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it," the secretary of State said. "But we would prefer to do it peacefully."
Meanwhile, Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said an agreement with the U.S. is possible if Washington "demonstrates goodwill" and is "truly seeking a peaceful solution," according to the state-owned Islamic Republic News Agency .
Araghchi said mediators are discussing the proposal Iran made during the United Nations General Assembly in September. Tehran expects the U.S. to lift sanctions, reduce its military presence in the region to previous levels and lift the blockade, the foreign minister said.
But Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei on Saturday called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
Concerns over the Middle East and Ukraine conflicts will likely linger in the near term.
"Attacks on ships and refineries in the Middle East and on civilians in Ukraine continue, doing little to inspire confidence in the prospects for lasting ceasefires in the foreseeable future," said Tamas Varga, analyst at PVM Oil Associates.
"Nonetheless, hope springs eternal," Varga added.
— CNBC's Lim Hui Jie contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Iran says "ball is in the U.S. court" on deal to end war as Trump keeps his intentions veiled
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Iran says "ball is in the U.S. court" on deal to end war as Trump keeps his intentions veiled
articles.content_orig:
Iran's top diplomat said Monday that negotiations with the U.S., via mediators, aimed at reaching an agreement to end the war have been "proceeding very intensively," but he added that "everything depends on Washington's political rationality," according to Iran's state news agency IRNA.
IRNA quoted Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi as reiterating that Tehran will not back down from its conditions for a deal to end the war and to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
Closed-door negotiations have taken place via mediators, primarily Qatar and Pakistan, and Iranian officials said earlier Monday that it would be up to the U.S. side to make a move and end the monthslong standoff sparked by the joint U.S. and Israeli strikes on Feb. 28.
"If they choose honest diplomacy, we are ready to engage," IRNA quoted Araghchi as saying. "If they intend to deceive us and launch military operations, they will face a response more bitter and forceful than before."
The Iranian Navy claimed Monday that another oil tanker had caught on fire after striking a sea mine near the eastern entrance to the Strait of Hormuz, according to the Fars News Agency, which is closely linked with Iran's powerful Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
The report cited the Navy as saying the unnamed vessel had struck a mine while attempting to use shipping lanes through the strait that Iran considers unauthorized and unsafe, but which the Trump administration and U.S. military have repeatedly claimed are free and open.
The tanker had switched off its navigation systems, Fars said, referring to a common practice by commercial vessels trying to obscure their movements in the region.
Tanker owners should take a lesson from the fate of vessels that violate Iran's rules by trying to transit the strait without authorization from Tehran, the report cited the navy as saying.
On Friday, despite repeated assurances from the U.S. that the southern shipping lanes through the strait are open and safe to navigate, the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said there had been 30 attacks on commercial vessels in the region in the month of October alone, a record high.
The Iranian regime said earlier Monday that 11 ships had "caught fire" in or near the Strait of Hormuz in the last nine days alone.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Saturday that Tehran had presented Qatari mediators with a proposal to shorten the implementation period of a potential deal with the U.S. to just two days from seven.
In an interview with Al Jazeera , Araghchi said: "The Qatari side proposed shortening the implementation period of the Iranian proposal to five days. We have reached a proposal at this stage that reduces the implementation period to two days."
The Iranian minister added, however, that Tehran's conditions for a deal to end the war remain the same.
The Islamic Republic regime has demanded that the U.S. release frozen Iranian financial assets, lift the naval blockade of Iranian ports, as well as sanctions, and cease hostilities on all fronts, including Israel's battle with Hezbollah in Lebanon and Hamas in Gaza. In exchange, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping traffic and commit to further talks on its nuclear program.
Under the original seven-day implementation proposed by Tehran, the Strait of Hormuz would have been reopened on the sixth day.
With the shortened implementation period, according to a statement on the Iranian government website, "a series of measures will be taken by the United States on the first day, and on the second day, the Strait of Hormuz will reopen and maritime traffic will return to its previous conditions."
Iran's government-run broadcaster IRIB said Monday that 11 oil tankers had "caught fire" in the Strait of Hormuz in the previous nine days, disputing U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper's assertion last week that "all primary transit routes in the Strait of Hormuz remain free and clear."
In a post on X, IRIB said the 11 tankers had caught on fire since Oct. 25, the day on which it claimed Cooper made his recent fly-over of the strait.
The Iranian network offered no evidence, but claimed some of the vessels sank "to the depths of the sea."
Since the start of the war in February, Iran has targeted vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz in an effort to assert control over the narrow waterway, through which about a fifth of the world's crude oil supply typically passed prior to the conflict.
Cooper said last week in a Friday video statement that he saw no Iranian navy vessels in the strait during his flyover earlier in the week.
Later Friday, however, the U.K. navy's Maritime Trade Operations center said there had been 30 attacks on commercial vessels in the month of October alone, a record high.
The U.S. military and President Trump have repeatedly declared Iran's navy destroyed and insisted that southern shipping lanes through the strait are available to merchant vessels, but ongoing Iranian threats and attacks have kept the risks and costs for shippers high, which has helped Tehran keep maintain pressure on global energy prices.
Iranian officials repeated warnings Monday of possible gas shortages for residents ahead of the winter, and they called on people to conserve the resource.
First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref said he had to be honest about the stability of Iran's gas network in the colder months, as he asked the public to help conserve it.
Aref cited "imbalances accumulated over previous years and war-related damages," and warned that prices would increase for consumers who fail to conserve.
It is not the first time an Iranian official has warned about shortages. On October 25 , Iran's parliament speaker said natural gas consumption across Iran had to be reduced by 10%.
Iran's economy has been devastated by years of international sanctions, and the U.S. turn to economic warfare after the initial bombing campaigns of the ongoing conflict have strained finances for Tehran even further. The regime has not shown any willingness to bend on its demands to end the war, however, despite the economic pain for most Iranians.
Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson said Monday that the next move in the standoff with the United States is for President Trump to make.
"The ball is in the U.S. court, because our demands have been stated very clearly and transparently, and Iran's demands are reasonable and logical," Esmaeil Baqaei told journalists in Tehran.
Baqaei said ongoing negotiations, which have been brokered by Qatar, Pakistan and other mediators, were centered around the a seven-day proposal that Iran originally presented to the U.S. side in September, which calls for frozen Iranian assets to be released, the U.S. naval blockade to be lifted and an end to fighting on all fronts, in exchange for the phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and further negotiations on other topics.
President Trump rejected the initial proposal, but both sides have since exchanged revisions, and Mr. Trump has said repeatedly in recent weeks that he just needs to make a decision on whether to launch new attacks on Iran, or to make a deal to end the war.
Speaking Sunday to a radio network ahead of a campaign rally in Iowa, Mr. Trump said he would finish with the war soon, "one way or the other."
"Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it," he said, without offering any further context.
President Trump told reporters Sunday that he'd spoken with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Saturday and had a "very good talk with him."
Mr. Trump gave no details but said the two had discussed the war in Iran.
According to sources cited by Axios , Netanyahu pushed for Mr. Trump to strike Iran but the president wants to let the negotiations play out.
The U.S. and Iran both engaged in indirect talks via mediators led by Qatar who are pushing to strike a deal between both sides before the conflict escalated.

articles.title_orig: Labour to end power-sharing with Greens in 11 councils over Zionism row
articles.title_zh: Labour to end power-sharing with Greens in 11 councils over Zionism row
articles.content_orig:
Deals with six Green council groups that have condemned the motion are to remain in place, says Labour
UK politics live – latest updates
Labour is to stop cooperating with the Green party in 11 councils across England following an ultimatum for Greens in local government to disown a new policy stating that “Zionism is racism”.
A statement from Labour said coalitions or other deals with Greens would stop in all local authorities where they had refused to condemn the policy motion passed at their party conference last month, which also called for a single Palestinian state in place of Israel.
Cooperation would cease on Arun, Derbyshire Dales, Havant, Lewes, Sheffield, Stafford, Warwick, Wealden, West Devon and West Suffolk councils, Labour said, and had already stopped in Runnymede because of the motion.
According to Labour, six Green council groups have condemned the motion, meaning deals will remain in place in Broadland, Monmouthshire, North Somerset, Rother, West Oxfordshire, West Sussex. The same, it said, had happened with the West of England mayoralty, where the mayor is from Labour and the deputy mayor is a Green.
Bridget Phillipson, the Labour chair, said the party had been clear that the motion, which has been met with unease by some Greens and has faced significant outside condemnation , “crosses a line and we cannot work with any party that supports it – at any level of government”.
The Greens said they were “hugely disappointed” at the move, saying it would result in worse outcomes for residents in affected areas.
Phillipson said just over a fortnight ago that any Labour groups working with Green party politicians should review their agreements and end them unless they reject the motion, which Andy Burnham called “antisemitic” .
Some Greens, including the party’s former co-leader Adrian Ramsay, had called on local parties to renounce the policy, a stance that put him at odds with Zack Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales. The party’s official response was that the Greens would “not take lectures” from a Labour government that supplies arms to Israel.
The policy equates Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, with racism. It also rejects a two-state solution and calls for Israel to be replaced by a single Palestinian state “with equal rights for all”.
The Equality and Human Rights Commission has written to the Greens to seek more information about the motion “and assess its practical implications and potential impact”.
Phillipson said: “Any local power-sharing arrangement cannot come at the expense of upholding the moral obligation we have to stand up for everyone in our communities and the values we share.
“We are pleased that some local Green parties have rightly opted to disavow this policy and have called on their party’s leadership to do the same. It is disappointing that some local Green parties have not met the conditions Labour has set out. Labour continues to oppose this divisive policy and calls on the Green party to do the right thing and rescind it.”
after newsletter promotion
She added: “The Labour party fought hard to root out antisemitism within our own party and ensure it had no place in our politics.”
In a joint statement, the Greens and the Local Government Association Green group said they were “hugely disappointed in moves designed by national parties to force local council leaders into jeopardising successful progressive partnerships that are delivering benefits for residents”.
They added: “Across the country, Green, Labour, independent and Liberal Democrat councillors have worked together to provide stable local government, protect services and deliver positive change. Leaders across these parties are rightly proud of what those partnerships have achieved.
“Those who issued ultimatums that destabilised power-sharing agreements have often ignored the judgments of their own local leaders, failed to respect the choices made by local voters, and are disrupting successful partnerships.”
Under the party’s direct democracy rules, policy is decided by party members. The Zionism motion won just over 1,000 votes, equating to approximately 0.4% of the total membership. It has been criticised by four of the Greens’ five MPs, as well as the former MP and party leader Caroline Lucas.
On Sunday, Ramsay said the Greens must fix their internal democracy to avoid a takeover by the hard left, saying some new members “might be more at home” in Your Party or the Socialist Workers party.

articles.title_orig: Supermarket freezers across Europe hit by second suspected cyber-attack
articles.title_zh: Supermarket freezers across Europe hit by second suspected cyber-attack
articles.content_orig:
Chains in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg say fridge temperatures rose overnight, similar to hack of French stores
Supermarket chains in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg have said the temperatures of their refrigerators and freezers in dozens of stores rose overnight, prompting fears of a cyber-attack similar to one that caused millions of euros of food losses in France.
Sweden’s Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet on Monday that six of ​its stores ‌had been ​affected, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”.
The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​cybersecurity ‌incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said an “IT incident” ​had hit fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg.
A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the supermarket chain had established that temperatures in the cooling systems had increased, adding that the incident was being investigated.
Belgium’s Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of stores and supermarkets were affected, including five Spar outlets, multiple Shop & Go convenience stores attached to Q8 service stations, and a number of smaller Proxy Delhaize minimarkets.
“We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which specialises in refrigeration system installations, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations from the grid.”
French ⁠police said in October that hackers had seized control of cooling units at ⁠up to 700 supermarkets in a large-scale attack that led to heavy losses of chilled and frozen foods and underlined the vulnerability of internet-connected systems.
Hackers had remotely overridden the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C. The Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains were among those affected.
Stores had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products, with many suffering losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000). Two stores in Alsace reported a combined loss of €270,000.
Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures. In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss.
after newsletter promotion
They disabled alarm systems before adjusting the thermostats or extending the defrost programme by hours. Danfoss said it had identified security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates.
The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigatiion into the French attack, saying damage included “food losses and fires”, and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, to investigate.
ANSSI subsequently confirmed that supermarkets using controllers from two other companies were also targeted in the attack.

articles.title_orig: America’s Gulf Allies Prepare for New Round of Strikes on Iran—and the Blowback
articles.title_zh: America’s Gulf Allies Prepare for New Round of Strikes on Iran—and the Blowback
articles.content_orig:
Third day of indirect talks as Qatar tries to negotiate release of $6bn in Iranian assets that could lead to waterway’s reopening
Officials from the Gulf states are “braced for the worst” as they wait for Washington’s response to an Iranian proposal that could reopen the strait of Hormuz before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
Indirect talks in Doha ran into a third day on Sunday with Qatar trying to negotiate the release of more than $6bn in Iranian assets, which could lead to the reopening of the strait of Hormuz and the restart of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme.
The United Arab Emirates envoy Anwar Gargash said another round of escalation was not in the interests of Iran or any of its neighbours. He said: “We are also, as we have shown before, braced for the worst.”
He added: “Relations with Iran are essential, because Iran is our neighbour and we do not want to see it get caught up in a prolonged crisis.”
Qatar’s mediation continued despite unidentified missiles striking a Pakistan-bound Qatari LNG tanker near the strait of Hormuz on Friday. The attack came despite the ship receiving direct clearance and safe-passage approval from Tehran just hours earlier.
In a bid to overcome the lack of trust on both sides, Qatar has been focusing its efforts on reaching an agreement for a plan to compress the process by which the US lifts sanctions and then Iran reopens the strait of Hormuz and starts nuclear talks. Iran has agreed to cut the timetable from seven to two days.
Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said he hoped the US would choose “diplomacy over other paths”. He said Iran was ready for both defence and diplomacy, depending on Washington’s “rationality”. Araghchi said there were currently no plans for direct talks with Washington.
Araghchi has not been attending the mediation in Doha and is due to go to Turkmenistan on Monday, but other Iranian diplomats are heavily involved.
Donald Trump said on Saturday the US had knocked out much of Iran’s military but still had to “take care of” one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked. He maintained that negotiations with Iran to end the war, started by the US and Israel in February, were “going fine but you know they’re not very reliable”.
Earlier on Saturday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US was open to a diplomatic solution, while Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, disclosed that he had received a letter from the US vice-president, JD Vance, seeking to revive talks.
Rezaei noted what he described as a positive change in “tone” from the US side but said he had yet to respond.
Speaking to Al Jazeera on Saturday, Araghchi said Iran had offered to open the strait of Hormuz within two days of the US acting to lift the blockade on oil ships, stop blocking the release of Iranian assets and end sanctions on Iranian oil exports.
Ali Nikzad, the deputy speaker of Iran’s parliament, once again signalled that Tehran would be unwilling to discuss its nuclear programme, saying: “Our enemies must understand that the Iranian nation has made a decision not to negotiate on the nuclear issue under any circumstances or under any pressure. This great nation gave its enemies enough opportunity to negotiate in this area, but was faced with repeated breaches of promises and illegal bombing of part of peaceful nuclear facilities.”
Rezaei claimed Trump was being hounded by a war that he claimed was having wider international repercussions than the Vietnam war. He told Iranian TV on Saturday: “Today, wherever Trump goes, he must answer why he started the war against Iran. There is no family in America that has not endured the pressure caused by the war in Iran.”

articles.title_orig: Shabana Mahmood to set out changes to settlement rules for legal migrants
articles.title_zh: Shabana Mahmood to set out changes to settlement rules for legal migrants
articles.content_orig:
Shabana Mahmood scraps plans for migrant care workers already in the UK to wait 15 years for permanent settlement - watch her speaking in the Commons live above
As long as they earn at least Â£25,000 and arrived in the UK before May 2025, these workers will be eligible for indefinite leave to remain (ILR)  after five years
Mahmood also drops the requirement for any low income workers to wait for 15 years before getting ILR, reducing it to 10
She previously proposed extending the wait from the current five years to 10, in response to a period of high net migration, but has faced opposition from within her own party for proposing to apply the changes to migrant workers already in the UK
The Conservatives have said that any watering down of the proposal would be a "slap in the face to British taxpayers"
Indefinite leave to remain (ILR) , also known as settlement, gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible
Edited by Kieran Kelly and Manish Pandey
Mahmood says rights granted under settlement, including access to the NHS and education, should "not be automatic, it should be earned".
She adds the current system, under which people can apply for settlement after 5 years, does not represent true fairness.
The home secretary sets out what the government considers to be disqualifying criteria for settlement
She says that a five-year path to settlement will remain open to all higher earners on a salary over Â£50,000 and those who have made contributions in healthcare and education.
In the Commons, Shabana Mahmood begins her statement by saying she promised at the recent Labour Party conference that the country would adopt a migration policy that is "guided above all by fairness".
The home secretary says her parents came to the UK over 50 years ago from rural Kashmir, adding that it is her responsibility that the country's migration system lives on an ideal of fairness.
She says the UK "welcomes those who seek a new and better life within it", but there is an expectation they will play their part, contribute to their community and became a part of the country's national life.
"Solidarity is the precondition for social  justice," she adds.
The home secretary has scrapped a plan for migrant social care workers already in the country to wait 15 years before getting indefinite leave to remain (ILR).
As long as those workers earn at least Â£25,000 and arrived in the UK before May 2025 they will be eligible for ILR after five years.
Shabana Mahmood has also dropped the requirement for any low income workers to wait for 15 years before getting ILR. She has reduced the requirement to all other low income workers to 10 years.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is now up in the House of Commons, where she is due to set out changes to settlement rules for legal migrants.
We'll bring you all her key news lines here - you can also follow along by tapping watch live at the top of the page.
Chris Mason Political editor
At the heart of the debate around legal migration are contested notions of fairness.
Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood has talked of her parents coming to the UK from rural Kashmir. Now, this daughter of immigrants is responsible for reshaping the very system that brought them here decades ago â and doing so in a way that both her party and the country regard as fair.
"Fair to those who seek a new and better life here, like my parents did. And fair to those already here, including British workers, and especially the young," is how Mahmood put it in her speech to the Labour Party conference in September.
The debate has come at a time of huge legal immigration in recent years and during a period in which Reform UK have been particularly prominent in the national political conversation.
Both of these things are factors in Labour wanting to be seen to be taking people's concerns about the scale of arrivals seriously.
But her political opponents smell what they see as weakness and retreat, with parts of her original plan now being revised, as the BBC's Iain Watson reported over the weekend.
You can read Chris Mason's full analysis here.
The most recent immigration figures showed net migration was at its lowest level since 2012, excluding the Covid pandemic.
Data released by the Office for National Statistics (ONS) in May showed that migration added 171,000 people to the UK's population last year, almost half the number seen in 2024.
The data also revealed that 93,525 people claimed asylum in the UK in the year to March 2026 - down 12% on the year prior, but still more than double that seen just before the pandemic.
The ONS said net migration continued to fall to levels last seen in early 2021 - when a new immigration system was introduced and Covid travel restrictions were in place.
Policy changes from early 2024 under the former Conservative government are likely to have made an impact on the net migration figures, including most overseas students being restricted from bringing family members to the UK.
The Labour government has retained the measures and in some cases expanded on them, including by introducing plans to end the recruitment of overseas care workers.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham says it's "difficult to say" whether legal migration is too high or low in a recorded interview aired ahead of the home secretary's Commons address.
Speaking to ITV, Burnham said legal migration had "come right down" after official data released in May showed net migration had dropped to 171,000 in 2025, nearly half that of the previous year.
"I think when you have planned migration it's difficult to say whether it's too high or too
low because it's got to be, if you like, following gaps in the economy, because if you
just put a number on it we may have a shortage in a certain area," he said.
However, he said migration overall was in a "much better place" as small boat crossing were also down, with 22,128 arrivals so far this year up to 31 October, down 40% from the same period last year.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic Revenue Hits Nearly $17 Billion Before Blockbuster IPO
articles.title_zh: Anthropic Revenue Hits Nearly $17 Billion Before Blockbuster IPO
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Anthropic's first operating profit lasted one quarter. Its computing bill, nearly $900 billion, is just getting started.
The maker of Claude ( ANTH.PVT ) put a total on that bill for the first time Monday. Its amended IPO filing lists about $895 billion of commitments, nearly all of it for computing and data centers. About $70 billion comes due within a year. The full bill is almost seven times the roughly $132 billion of cash and short-term investments Anthropic held at the end of September.
The filing also added third quarter results. Revenue jumped to about $17 billion from $11.6 billion in the second quarter. But Anthropic reported a $567 million operating loss , one quarter after its first operating profit of $974 million.
Anthropic books most of its computing 12 to 18 months ahead. When demand ran past that capacity last quarter, it bought $5 billion of short-term computing that "currently costs significantly more" than its long-term deals, the filing says. A $2 billion non-cash charge tied to a donation-matching program added to the loss.
Three days before the filing, Seaport Research Partners analyst Jay Goldberg warned on Yahoo Finance that the profits wouldn't last.
"They will be profitable probably in the next quarter or two. But then they're going to start going back into losses," he said.
Nearly $450 billion of the commitments come due by the end of 2030. Purchase commitments alone jumped to about $314 billion from $55 billion at the end of 2025. Broadcom (AVGO) tops the list with about $161 billion in equipment leases. Alphabet's ( GOOGL ) Google is next at about $121 billion, up from $114.5 billion in the first filing. SpaceX's ( SPCX ) AI unit follows at up to $120.5 billion, then Amazon ( AMZN ) at $110 billion.
Anthropic also plans another $125 billion to $150 billion of Google chips and expects to spend more than $20 billion with AMD (AMD). Neither deal has a fixed dollar commitment, so neither counts toward the $895 billion.
That makes Anthropic one of the biggest customers the cloud giants have, and one of their rivals too.
"For the hyperscalers, Anthropic is at once a customer, competitor, sales channel and investment," Evercore ISI analyst Mark Mahaney wrote after the first filing.
Anthropic estimates that 5% to 7% of its revenue in the first nine months of the year came from customers who were breaking its usage policy or commercial terms. It stepped up enforcement in August and September and warned the crackdown "may reduce our overall revenue and growth rates in future periods."
Price cuts tied to new models and discounts also shaved about $600 million off third quarter revenue.
Some shares will be offered through Charles Schwab (SCHW), Fidelity, Robinhood (HOOD), SoFi (SOFI) and Morgan Stanley's ( MS ) E*Trade, the filing says. The price range and share count are still blank.
Buyers will also face dilution . Anthropic has 1.77 billion stock options outstanding and has set aside up to 2.95 billion shares for a new equity plan.
"Certainly it's a pretty challenging setup for their IPO," Goldberg said.

articles.title_orig: Marvell to buy Lumentum in $115 billion deal in AI data-center bet
articles.title_zh: Marvell to buy Lumentum in $115 billion deal in AI data-center bet
articles.content_orig:
Marvell Technology on Monday said it will buy optical components maker Lumentum to address growing connectivity demands from the artificial intelligence infrastructure buildout.
"AI infrastructure is undergoing a fundamental architectural shift toward optical connectivity, creating an opportunity that comes along once in a generation," said Marvell Chairman and CEO Matt Murphy in a release. "The companies that move first and help define this transition will set the standard for decades to come."
Since the tie-up is a fixed ratio deal with no cash, the value will depend on the price of Marvell shares. The company said the transaction has an implied enterprise value of $115 billion for Lumentum, in a release.
Through the acquisition, Marvell said it can combine electrical and optical technologies to meet accelerating and shifting AI connectivity demands across regions and systems. Companies are increasingly relying on optical connections to piece together chips used to run and train large language models.
Lumentum shareholders will receive 4.5 Marvell shares for each Lumentum share under the agreement. The deal is expected to close during the first half of 2028.
Marvell's takeover marks one of the most significant bets on AI in 2026 and comes despite recent concerns over the long-term sustainability of infrastructure spending.
This isn't the company's first bet on AI growth. This year, the company closed a multibillion-dollar deal for Celestial AI, a startup focused on optical interconnectivity technology.
Marvell has seen its market value more than triple over the last three years, buoyed by unrelenting AI enthusiasm. Lumentum's stock has more than doubled in 2026 alone.
Marvell shares slumped 3%, while Lumentum's stock declined about 4% before the bell.

articles.title_orig: Iran has a 2-day plan to reopen strait, resume nuclear talks with US, and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Iran has a 2-day plan to reopen strait, resume nuclear talks with US, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
The commander of the Revolutionary Guards in Tehran announced the formation of Iran's first Janfada brigade and said its fighters would soon be deployed to operational areas in southern and western Iran.
The Janfada initiative is part of the Islamic Republic's effort to mobilize civilians into organized paramilitary formations, providing military training and preparing them for potential combat and irregular warfare operations alongside the Revolutionary Guards.
Hassan Hassanzadeh said Monday that the first brigade had completed additional training and been equipped, with preparations underway for specialized live-fire exercises.
Speaking at the opening of the fourth Janfada training center in Tehran's Tajrish Square, he said further brigades and battalions would soon be organized based on their readiness.
Hassanzadeh also claimed that more than 33 million Iranians had expressed willingness to participate in the Janfada campaign, saying the scale of public participation had once again "surprised Iran's enemies."
Concerns over the lack of a centralized military intelligence structure in Iran have been addressed following instructions from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei to senior military commanders, lawmaker Mojtaba Zarei said.
Zarei, a member of parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, said Monday that Khamenei's directives on updating the military's target list had also emphasized the need to strengthen the country's military intelligence architecture.
He said the structure would enable Iranian forces to identify adversaries' military capabilities and plans, laying the groundwork for what he described as “severe and effective” strikes against them.
Khamenei's office said Saturday that he had ordered military commanders to update their target lists to bring a wider range of US and Israeli assets within Iran's reach.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Monday that consultations through Qatari and Pakistani mediators were "very intense" and that the Strait of Hormuz would reopen if the United States accepted Tehran's conditions, the state-run IRNA news agency reported.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, and Russian President Vladimir Putin discussed developments in the Middle East during a phone call, Iran's Revolutionary Guards-affiliated Fars news agency reported Monday.
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said Monday that the Persian Gulf region had again reached a "critical crossroads between war and peace," calling for an end to hostilities through negotiations.
Wang made the remarks during a meeting with Saudi Arabia's national security adviser in Beijing, according to a statement from China's Foreign Ministry.
He urged all parties to safeguard regional energy security and shipping routes, adding that China was ready to work with Saudi Arabia to make further progress in bilateral relations.
Oil prices fell nearly 6% Monday as talks between Iranian officials and Qatari mediators over ending the US-Israeli war on Iran raised hopes that disruptions to Middle East energy supplies could ease.
Brent crude futures dropped 5.9% to $106.76 a barrel, after rising more than 2% in the previous session.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Monday that the country's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei had granted the government "certain authorities" regarding peace talks with Washington, Iranian state media reported.
Pezeshkian added that Iran would seek to resolve the conflict with the United States through dialogue.
An Iranian lawmaker warned Monday that the United States could launch a high-intensity, short-duration attack on Iran if Tehran refuses to enter negotiations, saying Washington's military buildup in the region was more than a show of force.
"They want to use military threats to bring Iran to the negotiating table, and if Iran refuses, they may carry out an attack of high intensity and limited duration," Ahmad Bakhshayesh Ardestani, a member of parliament's National Security Committee, told the semi-official ISNA news agency.
Bakhshayesh said the deployment of large numbers of weapons, destroyers, aircraft carriers and refueling aircraft to the region could not be intended solely to demonstrate military power.
He also criticized the prolonged uncertainty between war and diplomacy, saying the situations of "neither war nor peace" and "neither war nor negotiations" had become an unresolved problem that satisfied no one.
He said it was undesirable for Iran to remain unable to reach an agreement with Washington while facing naval, air and land blockades, economic pressure and psychological campaigns that were taking a toll on the population's mental well-being.
An oil tanker caught fire after striking a mine in the eastern part of the Strait of Hormuz, Iranian state media reported Monday.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian called for greater public involvement in running the country at a meeting with provincial governors and mayors of major cities on Monday.
“We can emerge powerfully from all the threats the enemy is creating,” he said. “Even if they assassinate thousands like me, if the people are with us, they can’t do a thing.”
Pezeshkian said people needed to believe officials intended to serve them and that public participation was essential to overcoming threats. He urged governors not to wait for government directives, but to coordinate locally and involve people in solving problems.
He said a village head could sometimes help the government more than a governor, and called for greater use of local resources. He also urged officials to prevent production units from closing and provide services at lower cost in disadvantaged areas.

Oil Prices Plunge as Draft Proposal to End U.S.-Iran War is Circulated
Charles is a writer for Oilprice.com
Oil prices extended losses from Asian trade into early Monday morning U.S. time as a draft proposal on a potential end to the U.S.-Iran war is now being circulated after Iranian negotiators left Qatar, an official briefed on the talks told Reuters on Monday.
Oil prices slumped by 3% in Asian trade on Monday amid renewed optimism about a possible peace deal between the United States and Iran, following reports about mediation talks between Iran and Qatar over the weekend.
Iranian negotiators left Qatar on Sunday and a draft proposal is now being circulated for a potential follow-up meeting, the Reuters source said, without elaborating on what the draft proposal could possibly entail.
“Lingering hopes of some form of diplomatic progress, combined with the absence of any meaningful military escalation over the weekend, have taken some of the immediate heat out of prices for now,” KCM Trade’s chief market analyst Tim Waterer said, as quoted by Reuters earlier today.
“Our demands have been articulated very clearly and transparently,” Reuters quoted Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Esmaeil Baghaei, as saying.
“These demands are reasonable and logical: no final agreement can be initiated, nor can the Strait of Hormuz be reopened or secured, unless the US naval blockade is brought ‌to an end, Iran's demands are respected, and Iran’s legitimate requirements are addressed,” the Iranian official said.
Iran this weekend said that the Strait of Hormuz could reopen within two days if its demands are met, faster than the week for reopening Tehran had aired in September.
U.S. President Donald Trump rejected Iran’s September proposal.
“It remains to be seen whether this will lead to anything,” ING’s commodities analysts Warren Patterson and Ewa Manthey said in a Monday note, commenting on the Iran-Qatar mediation talks.
Early on Monday, Brent Crude prices had dropped to $108.61, per barrel, down by 4.25% on the day, and WTI Crude slumped by 4.32% to below $100 a barrel, at $99.62.
Still, the market is apprehensive that new U.S.-Israel strikes on Iran could follow the U.S. midterm elections.
“Given that many of the key developments in this conflict have unfolded over weekends, the market may have to hold its breath until the end of the week,” ING’s strategists said.

articles.title_orig: Mystery skeleton at Westminster Abbey was likely an abbot buried in a secondhand sarcophagus
articles.title_zh: Mystery skeleton at Westminster Abbey was likely an abbot buried in a secondhand sarcophagus
articles.content_orig:
A centuries-old stone coffin discovered more than 150 years ago at London’s Westminster Abbey sparked a question that has endured ever since: Who’s inside? Now, archaeologists have clues that point to a respected medieval figure who was not the burial’s original occupant.
Prior research had determined that the sarcophagus dated to the Roman period, around the fourth century, and a three-line Latin inscription dedicated it “to the memory of Valerius Amandinus.” Given the coffin’s high quality, Amandinus was probably an important resident of London, but nothing is known about his life and deeds.
DNA evidence from Thomas Jefferson’s hair reveals the truth about his relationship with Sally Hemings
However, a cross of a late Anglo-Saxon style carved on the sarcophagus lid and measuring 5.9 feet (1.8 meters) long was likely made at least 600 years later. The symbol’s presence sowed doubts about the age and identity of the skeleton inside, according to Warwick Rodwell, a consultant archaeologist at Westminster Abbey.
He conducted a new analysis of the remains and found the coffin’s occupant was likely a medieval monk or abbot of Westminster. Rodwell reported his findings October 20 in the Journal of the British Archaeological Association .
Workers first discovered the burial at the abbey in 1820. During its excavation, they broke the lid into six pieces, and their rough handling damaged the skull. The bones were swept into a pile and left in disarray, perhaps disturbed by looters while the lid was open. Then, the coffin and its contents were reburied without being catalogued or studied.
The sarcophagus was “found” a second time in 1869 during a renovation project, and it was moved from the abbey’s North Green region to the East Cloister. (Charles Dickens Jr., eldest son of the famous novelist, wrote about seeing the sarcophagus at the abbey in 1879, according to the study.) It was later relocated to the base of the abbey’s northwest tower, a task that took more than 36 hours due to the coffin’s weight.
Rodwell first learned of the coffin’s history in 2009. When he found out that the sarcophagus was scheduled for cleaning and conservation in 2016, in preparation for display in new galleries that were being constructed in the abbey, he seized the rare chance to revisit the mysterious burial.
“I saw this as an opportunity to take a fresh look at it, and to see what was inside — if anything — after 150 years of being sealed up,” he told CNN in an email.
Rodwell found the bones were still jumbled together inside the coffin, which was hewn from a single block of limestone and measured about 7 feet (2 meters) long, with walls about 4 inches (10 centimeters) thick on average. The skeleton was about 90% complete, and the skull had been reconstructed when the coffin was last opened in 1869, he wrote in the study.
George Washington family secrets revealed by DNA from unmarked 19th century graves
Skeletal analysis hinted that this was a man who died between the ages of 35 and 49 years, and radiocarbon dating of the bones placed him between A.D. 987 and 1052. His teeth were in good condition. And while some bones showed evidence of healed fractures, osteoarthritis and gout, there was no sign of serious disease or injury that might have caused the man’s death.
When the researchers removed the skeleton and cleared the coffin of soil and rubble, they were surprised to find a rectangular patch of lime, a compound thought to accelerate decay and trap “miasmas,” so-called toxic vapors that were erroneously linked to disease. The shape of the lime patch suggested that the body had been inside a rectangular wooden coffin that was then filled with lime before being placed in the sarcophagus, Rodwell said. “This had not been suspected, and the timber coffin had totally rotted away.”
The practice of covering a body in lime was rare in the Middle Ages and typically reserved for high-status burials, he added.
That clue and the cross on the coffin led the researchers to reason that the skeleton probably belonged to an important man, most likely the abbot of Westminster. Two historically identified candidates arose for that period: Ælfwig, abbot from A.D. 993 to around 1020, and Wulfnoth, who became abbot in 1020. Ælfwig is a slightly stronger contender, according to the study, as he was known to have been a monk at Westminster before becoming abbot and may therefore have had a clearer connection to the church.
“No single clue clinched the matter,” Rodwell said. “It was a case of assembling and weighing all the strands of evidence.”
But why would the abbot of a prestigious church be buried in a used Roman coffin? Rodwell said this could actually be a tribute to his elevated status.
“In the late Saxon period stone coffins were hard to come by — the industry for making them had died out,” he said. “Acquiring a secondhand stone coffin was considered a ‘prize.’”
So valued were these coffins, he added, that in the seventh century, British monks from an abbey in Ely traveled to a Roman cemetery in Cambridge and dug up a stone coffin to take back with them for their deceased abbess, Æthelthryth.
‘Bone biographies’ reveal what life was like for everyday medieval people
Another example of a repurposed stone coffin is the elaborate fourth century sarcophagus currently in the Vatican Museums that is rumored to hold the remains of Helena, mother of the emperor Constantine the Great, said Dr. Simon Roffey, a reader in medieval archaeology at the University of Winchester in the UK. Carved with a military scene of Roman soldiers trampling barbarians, the coffin was likely intended for a man.
Still, further research is needed to fully explain the motives and rationale behind the reuse of pagan tombs and sarcophagi during the medieval Christian period, Roffey told CNN in an email. He was not involved in the new research.
While Ælfwig the abbot isn’t exactly a well-known figure who looms large in the public imagination, this discovery nonetheless untangled a mystery that has stymied academics since 1869 and fills a significant gap in the Anglo-Saxon history of Westminster Abbey, “the most important church in Britain,” Rodwell said.
Mindy Weisberger is a science writer and media producer whose work has appeared in Live Science, Scientific American and How It Works magazine. She is the author of “ Rise of the Zombie Bugs : The Surprising Science of Parasitic Mind-Control” (Hopkins Press).

articles.content_orig:
The top configuration of the Raspberry Pi 5 now costs three times more than its launch price.﻿
The top configuration of the Raspberry Pi 5 now costs three times more than its launch price.﻿
The Raspberry Pi 5 with 16GB of RAM now costs $385 after an $80 price hike , the latest in a string of increases driven by the ongoing RAM shortage . This configuration launched at $120 and now costs more than triple that price. The 16GB versions of the Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5 also got a $40 price hike and now cost between $375 and $415.
According to Raspberry Pi CEO Eben Upton, these price hikes were driven specifically by a lack of “alternative supply” for 16GB DRAM, on top of shortages for other components. Upton says, “Though these increases are unavoidable, we know they are unwelcome news for our customers. We encourage you to make sure you’re not paying for more memory than you need.” Upton suggested using Pis with less memory or older Pi models as alternatives to the pricey 16GB model. Unfortunately, other Raspberry Pi 5 configurations have also gotten more expensive — the 2GB version got a price hike last month.
At $385, the 16GB Raspberry Pi 5 is nearing the price of a desktop mini PC. Upton reiterated the company’s plans to reverse the price hikes, saying, “the current memory landscape is difficult but ultimately temporary, and we look forward to rolling back our price increases when memory costs fall once again.”

articles.title_orig: Inside White Dwarf 530 – The forces of the Ten Thousand unleashed
articles.title_zh: Inside White Dwarf 530 – The forces of the Ten Thousand unleashed
articles.content_orig:
Inside White Dwarf 530 – The forces of the Ten Thousand unleashed
Custodes take point in a White Dwarf featuring Ancestor Gods, space pirates and titanic, duelling walkers. Join us as we take a look inside.
Issue 530 kicks off with a lore article exploring Custodian titles and some of the heroic deeds they perform to earn them. Basically, if you ever meet a Custodian, don’t worry about not being able to remember their name!
Once that’s whetted your appetite, you get to see the forces of the Adeptus Custodes in action in a battle report pitting them against an insidious uprising of Genestealer cultists, whose very existence threatens the security of an entire subsector. Or it would if they could shoot straight with their mining lasers.
Worried your kill teams have had it too easy lately? The Tyrant’s Claim introduces a new Joint Ops mission for Kill Team, which finds your forces attempting to hold the line against Huron Blackheart and a cast of his closest ne’er-do-wells. Can you stop them as they venture forth from the Maelstrom to raid your supply lines in the finest piratical tradition?
The White Dwarf team heads over to the Mortal Realms to dig up lots of information about the newest Warhammer Age of Sigmar faction – the Khazalite Holds. There’s background and lore, plus interviews with the team behind the art in the new battletome, and a step-by-step painting guide from the ’Eavy Metal team for the colours of Karak Angaraz.
And what would an issue of White Dwarf be without its namesake? Grombrindal returns with a new Legends warscroll for the main duardin himself, as well as rules for a new Army of Renown – Grombrindal’s Expedition. This army focuses on Old Whitebeard leading a force of like-minded duardin who are able to harness their pioneering spirit into potent tactical advantages.
White Dwarf 530 also features your usual favourites including The Bunker, scenarios of the month for Warhammer 40,000 and Warhammer Age of Sigmar, and handy tearout rules for the Stormsurge and Wraithknight in Titanic Duel.*
White Dwarf 530 is available to pre-order from Saturday. Never miss an issue– and get them delivered directly to your door, with fancy full-art covers – by signing up for a 12-month subscription .
* Download the free rules for Titanic Duel now.

articles.title_orig: Binance sees more than $4.6 billion in withdrawals after largest crypto hack in history
articles.title_zh: Binance sees more than $4.6 billion in withdrawals after largest crypto hack in history
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Binance has seen $3.64 billion in net outflows since it gradually restored user withdrawals following the largest crypto hack in history, which the FBI linked to North Korea.
The world's biggest cryptocurrency exchange said that it processed $4.649 billion in withdrawals and approximately $1.01 billion in deposits. Binance detailed that the resulting net outflows represent just 2.1% of its $171 billion in total assets under management.
Binance was hit late Thursday by a hack that investigators said impacted roughly $6.3 billion in funds, with roughly half of those assets frozen.
On Monday, the exchange said it has covered approximately 95% of the impacted amount. The outstanding 5% consists of smaller tokens outside of the top 10 cryptocurrencies, whose assets are less liquid and will take longer to source.
Here's what you need to know:
"We continue working with industry partners to complete the remaining acquisitions," Binance said in an update on X.
Over the weekend, the FBI said the attack was linked to North Korea.
"The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is releasing information advising the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) was responsible for the theft of more than $6 billion USD in virtual assets from cryptocurrency exchange Binance, on or about October 29, 2026," a press release said.
Customer withdrawals were temporarily suspended, and co-CEO Richard Teng promised the exchange will cover all losses.
Teng said the hack was not carried out by one person. Initial findings pointed to a compromised laptop, but further review revealed broader security breaches.
"This was a complex attack," Teng said. "The attacker also used a self-destruct mechanism that destroyed tooling and tracers."
Around $3.24 billion remains in addresses linked to the theft, according to Tom Robinson, chief scientist and co-founder at blockchain analytics company Elliptic.
The attack has rattled crypto markets, and bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) traded at around $77,700 on Monday. Meanwhile, the total crypto market has lost roughly 3% in value, or $80 billion, over the last seven days, according to CoinMarketCap data.
Other major crypto assets also tumbled after the hack, with ether ( ETH-USD ) dropping to roughly $2,200. Binance's native token, BNB ( BND-USD ), also fell.

articles.title_orig: Karl Bushby completes 28-year, 31,000-mile walk around world and returns to mother’s house
articles.title_zh: Karl Bushby completes 28-year, 31,000-mile walk around world and returns to mother’s house
articles.content_orig:
Hull, England - For 28 years and one day, Karl Bushby took the long way home on an epic odyssey of human endurance back to northern England.
His adventure was made even more difficult - physically and mentally - with his two self-imposed guiding rules: he could not advance his journey with the help of any machine and he could not return home during the entire time, even if family or friends died.
It was also hardly a direct route. His journey was delayed at various times for months, if not years, by illness, visa restrictions in Russia, Moscow's invasion of Ukraine and having to swim massive bodies of water. His life was also threatened by armed gangs in the lawless Darien Gap in Central America, jail in Panama and a polar bear in Siberia.
Starting out at 29, he sported golden locks in his earliest pictures. Now 57, his beard is salt-and-pepper, and the elements and time weather his face.
On Monday, he took his final steps of an estimated 75 million to a hometown hero's welcome of claps and cheers as he walked into Hull, a gritty and proud working-class port city.
"I didn't do this alone. There was a big team, the biggest team: Earth. That's what it took to get me back," said Bushby to the assembled well-wishers in Hull, a working-class port city about 150 miles north of London.
"You wouldn't believe just how many people have been involved in this, to get us around the kinds of obstacles that we faced. We faced down governments. We faced down some of the hardest challenges. We've had to create two world records just to get back here. And I couldn't have done it on my own. So it was a world, global effort."
Bushby began what came to be known as his "Goliath Expedition" in Chile on Nov. 1, 1998. He made his way north through Central America, the United States and Canada, then crossed the Bering Sea to Russia in the world's first recorded attempt. He then carried on through Central Asia and swam for 31 days across the Caspian Sea in another reported first, in order to circumvent the war in Ukraine.
Over the past few years, he crossed Europe, and just last month, he swam from France across the English Channel, setting foot on the country of his birth where British immigration officers had set up to check his passport.
"It's almost like arriving in a foreign country," Bushby told CBS News over the weekend as he neared home. "I've worked with dollars for 28 years. I don't know the brands in the stores. So I'm going around wondering what I'm going to be buying. A couple of times I got caught out crossing the road because I'm looking in the other direction because these people drive on the wrong side of the road."
His home stretch Monday, quite literally, was a roughly 3-mile brisk walk from near Hull's town center to a quiet, sprawling neighborhood to the north of two-story, red-brick terrace homes.
Children lined the turn to his mother's home and cheered while an honor guard led the way.
Bushby pushed the cart that had been with him for about 25 years the last few steps.
He then embraced his waiting mother on the street outside her home. The cheers quieted, and the two shared a moment in this homecoming.
Bushby said he feels like a man wondering what home truly means after spending a generation around the world.
"I'm home, but it's not the home that I'm used to now for so long. And it's an odd feeling. And I almost feel guilt," he said. "Like there are other parts of the world now that feel more like home to me. And now I'm going to be faced with this weird static thing."
Now, after more than 10,000 days away, Bushby faces a different task: processing it all.
Confronted with the question of whether the world had gotten better or worse, he acknowledged the troubles but did not give up on his optimism.
"The world's in a little bit messier time; there are more wars, you know," he told CBS News. "But it's all good. At the end of the day, we've been through worse. So we all need to breathe a little bit, get through the tough times; we're going to be just fine. My bet is on us, no matter what. My bet is on humanity."
His final advice for anyone wondering if they could also accomplish something extraordinary: dream bigger.
"Yeah, you can, because I'm nothing special. Maybe we need the art of dreaming big again. People seem to dream outside of a very confined space mentally at the world that they live in," he said.
"You've got to have that little confidence. You got to realize that you're more capable than you think you are. People constantly underestimate themselves. So that's the first step, I think. Dream big. Realize you're probably capable more than you'd think. If you take nothing else from this … take that!"

articles.title_orig: Spain train crash: US, Japan and Canada citizens among dead, authorities say
articles.title_zh: Spain train crash: US, Japan and Canada citizens among dead, authorities say
articles.content_orig:
The train disaster, one of Europe’s deadliest rail incidents this century, killed 69 people, including 54 Spaniards
Four US citizens and one each from Canada, Japan, Argentina, Mexico, Tunisia and the Czech Republic were among the 69 killed in last week’s high-speed train collision in Spain, authorities said.
Wednesday’s disaster – one of Europe’s deadliest rail accidents this century – has seen victims’ relatives endure an agonising wait as forensics teams identify the dead, sometimes from individual body parts.
A legal body set up to handle the identification work, made up of police and forensics experts, announced in a statement late on Sunday the 10 latest confirmed foreign victims.
It had already announced the deaths of a French and a Portuguese citizen, as well as that of 54 Spaniards.
All but three of the victims are now identified, the statement added.
Three reports for missing people remain active, the authorities said. They concern two Australians and one Japanese citizen.
“As the contacted families have expressed their wish to travel to Spain to carry out in-person identification, we are awaiting their arrival in the country,” the statement said.
The accident was Spain’s second high-speed train collision this year and raised fresh questions about the country’s rail safety, after a crash in the southern region of Andalusia in January killed 46 people.
The latest disaster struck when a service by state operator Renfe ploughed into the back of a stationary train belonging to Spanish company Iryo outside the central village of Urda, around 130km (80 miles) south of Madrid.
The failure of an automatic safety system halted all trains on a 63km stretch of track, but a control centre authorised the Renfe service to resume its journey while the other train was still.
The tragedy came one month before a 29 November general election in which Socialist leader Pedro Sánchez will seek to overcome unfavourable polls and extend his eight-year premiership.

articles.title_orig: Supermarket fridges in Sweden, Ireland overheat amid suspected cyberattacks
articles.title_zh: Supermarket fridges in Sweden, Ireland overheat amid suspected cyberattacks
articles.content_orig:
Suspected cyberattacks have triggered temperatures to rise in grocery store refrigeration systems in a growing number of countries across Europe.
Overnight temperature spikes were recorded in stores in Belgium, Estonia, Ireland, Luxembourg and Sweden. On Monday, retailers and authorities pointed to alleged cyberattacks that underscored the vulnerability of systems that once largely operated mechanically.
The head of ⁠⁠⁠⁠Sweden’s national cybersecurity centre, John Billow, confirmed on Monday to the Reuters news agency that the centre ⁠⁠⁠⁠is responding to ⁠⁠⁠⁠multiple incidents affecting store cooling systems.
“We have in recent weeks … identified that we have quite a lot of exposed operational technology devices in Sweden that we have been clear about the necessity to update or patch,” he said.
The temperature of freezers in several Swedish stores rose suddenly overnight, store operators ICA and Coop said, while Swedish retailer Axfood said freezers at a distribution centre for home delivery of groceries in the Gothenburg area were hacked.
SuperValu, Ireland’s third-largest supermarket chain, ⁠⁠⁠⁠said a specific model of refrigeration systems has been affected by a “cyber incident” at 13 of its 223 ⁠⁠⁠⁠stores.
The Belga news agency reported overnight temperature increases at dozens of ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠Ahold Delhaize stores in Belgium and Luxembourg. They were blamed on a cyberattack, according to the chief ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠executive ⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠⁠of refrigeration company,⁠ ⁠⁠⁠Sabcobel.
Stephan Moelans said the units’ evaporators were switched to defrost mode.
Also in Belgium, five Spar shops had their fridge systems attacked, said a spokesperson for Colruyt Group, which operates the franchise system.
In Estonia, at least one supermarket chain was affected, technology supplier Kitman Coldtech told public broadcaster ERR.
“This is very fresh, it happened this morning,” Kitman’s CEO Jann Mutso said, without naming the affected chain.
Ahold Delhaize reported a cybersecurity incident to Dutch police last month.
The cyberattack on refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets in France raised the temperature of fridges and freezers to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122F), spoiling food and causing fires at several stores.
One Swedish store said in a social media post on Monday that the temperature of its refrigerators and freezers had been set to the same temperature as during the cyberattack in France.
“We are aware that a limited number of stores were affected by an incident overnight, which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems,” a spokesperson for privately held ICA told Reuters in an email.
Kitman’s Mutso also said that temperatures at the Estonian chain were set to 50 degrees Celsius (122F).
Privately-held retailer Coop told Swedish daily Aftonbladet that six of its stores had been affected by similar incidents.
There has been no claim of responsibility for Monday’s attack, nor the one earlier in France.
However, the incidents help to increase concern regarding hybrid warfare stemming from Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the Iran-United States war.
European states have blamed Moscow for a growing number of incidents affecting infrastructure, including via cyberattacks, in recent months. Russia has repeatedly denied involvement in any sabotage or hybrid warfare operations.
European Commissioner for Agriculture and Food Christophe Hansen said the attacks were “a deliberate attempt ⁠to disrupt” EU food supplies and undermine public ‌confidence.
“These incidents show that cyberattacks ⁠can disrupt services, affect ⁠businesses and directly affect citizens’ ⁠daily lives”, a ⁠European Commission spokesperson ⁠said, stressing the importance of strengthening ‌cybersecurity across the bloc.
A spokesperson for The Centre for Cybersecurity Belgium told Al Jazeera that the rising number of cyberattack incidents, especially those resulting from the targeted use of AI, is an evolving trend.
However, they added, “we may never be able to identify … who is behind this attack”.

It’s Warhammer Day on Saturday, and it’s not just about celebrating our own miniatures – there are also sales and reveals for a world of video games, merch, and more on the cards.

The delightfully devious stealth platformer Deathmaster has its story trailer revealed today. The story centers around Vinheek, a powerless Skaven prisoner when we first meet him, who has plans for greatness. Vihneek is freed by Skiteek, a fellow assassin from Clan Skrell – but Vihneek’s savior is ultimately his new captor. Clan Skrell wields Vihneek as a weapon, forcing him to complete deadly contracts at all costs and with no mercy. Every target Vihneek kills propels him higher within the Clan Skrell’s ranks, but looming threats from rival clans swirl…
Deathmaster is coming to Steam , XBOX Series S|X, PlayStation 5, and Nintendo Switch 2 in 2027, so get your knives sharpened and prepare to claw your way to the top of the Eshin hierarchy.
Battlesector turns 5 this year and to celebrate, a free update is landing on Warhammer Day adding a new map, gameplay options, and a major rebalance of units across the game. XBOX Play Anywhere also goes live today.
The next big DLC, Courage and Catastrophe, is also coming on 14 December , adding a 13-mission story campaign and three new units into the oodles of content already available.
Loads more updates and announcements are happening across our licensed merch partners and video game partners, so we’re going to have a quick-fire dash through them.
Wētā Workshop are hard at work on the next stunningly detailed 1:10 scale Warhammer statue, and have prepared a little teaser. Can you guess who it is? You will have to wait until later this year to find out for sure.
The Warhammer 40,000 Character Encyclopedia by DK Books has been expanded, adding even more characters so you can learn about the movers and shakers in the 41st Millennium. Check out these new page spreads. You can pre- order now !
Displate has revealed metal posters featuring key art of the four factions from Dawn of War IV . Not only that, but they have also revealed Warhammer 40,000 Shards are coming soon. Shards are mini metal prints with three rarity levels, built for collecting. Keep an eye on Displate for more information.
If you’ve ever wanted to enjoy Warhammer Art at an even bigger scale then now is the time to do so. Triptych is a new three piece wall art format available from Warhammer Art, beginning with this stunning Armageddon artwork.
We’re just over a week away from the launch of Warhammer Survivors on 10 November , which gives us just enough time to tell you about two new characters who’ll be selling you weapons and artefacts in-game.
Lord-Magnate Brokk Grungsson flexes his mercantile ways in the Mortal Realms, while Technoarchaeologist Daedalosus helps uncover lost artefacts in the 41st Millennium.
Also, you can prepare for the release by checking out a range of new Warhammer Survivors gear from the Warhammer Merch Store !
Staying with the Warhammer Merch Store – give praise to the Dark Gods with a new Chaos banner (coming soon, subject to final approval). Plus, a profane offering of additions to a wide swathe of clothing and accessories including Dawn of War IV desk mats on top of the Survivors gear available from today.
Check out two new entrants from the next line of TOMY plushes – the Blood Angels Intercessor and an adorable Nurgling wearing its tongue as a scarf. They’re hitting shelves in 2027, along with more as-yet-unrevealed designs.
Collect new artefacts from the legendary First Founding Chapters courtesy of Starforged , who revealed a line of magnetic Space Marine helmets today displaying their unique iconography and modifications.
You may have noticed that Warhammer 40,000: Boltgun 2 is out now – go and give it a try! Developers Auroch Digital have announced today that a Nintendo Switch 2 version will be released on 19 November .
Discover classic artwork appearing on Warhammer Combat Cards from now until 6 November before they revert to their usual miniature appearances.  You can also use the code WARHAMMERDAY in-game to get a bounty of free cards, plasma, and coins.*
Fresh from decking out Warhammer fans in clothing from the Empire of Man, Warhammer Armoury turns its attention to the lands of Bretonnia with a first preview of their latest costume set. For the Lady!
Cubicle 7 Games is celebrating the launch of its all-new Fifth Edition of Warhammer Fantasy Roleplay ! The classic RPG turns 40 this year. You can pre-order the core rulebook now, and you'll get a free PDF copy to play immediately.
Danilo have revealed their new Warhammer 40,000 Calendar.

articles.title_zh: As reparations debate grows, Caribbean campaigners point to one British family's example
articles.content_orig:
