Andy Burnham is being urged to reject proposals to pay reparations for Britain’s historic involvement in the slave trade to Caribbean nations as the row over the issue intensifies.
Former foreign secretary Sir Malcolm Rifkind branded the suggestion “illogical” and warned they should be rejected.
It comes as pressure mounts on the prime minister from left-wing Labour MPs to agree to reparations after he said he was willing to consider a formal apology.
But Downing Street has also moved to deny claims that Mr Burnham is considering some payouts to recognise Britain’s historic involvement in the slave trade .
Sir Malcolm, who served as foreign secretary between 1995 and 1997 in Sir John Major’s government, agreed it was right for King Charles to use the Commonwealth summit to condemn slavery.
However, the Tory grandee warned that there is no historical justification for reparations.
He told The Independent : “Those transported as slaves by the British were not enslaved by the British. They had been enslaved by Arabs in North Africa and, also, by black states, chiefs and others in West Africa. If reparations are being demanded from the UK they should also be demanded from Algeria, Morocco, Mali, Nigeria, Ghana, Dahomey and other states with as much responsibility as the British.”
He added: “The demands ignore that Britain led the world in making illegal the transportation of slaves across the Atlantic.
“The demands ignore that the Royal Navy enforced the ban on transportation by not only stopping and liberating slaves on British ships but also those of other countries that were transporting slaves.”
He added: “Why are those demanding reparations not also demanding massive reparations from the USA which legalised slavery in half of the US until the US Civil War in the late 19th century? It’s illogical and should be rejected.”
However, pressure is mounting from MPs on the left of Labour who helped push Sir Keir Starmer out of office and support Mr Burnham as his replacement.
Clapham and Brixton Hill Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, who ran for Labour deputy leader last year, is pushing for the British state to recognise its historic responsibility for the slave trade.
She told The Independent : “The prime minister’s attention to the issue of reparations, and his recognition that Britain must engage with our international partners on this, is welcome.
“Given the stance taken by successive governments on this issue, it is important to see him accept that Britain’s role in African chattel slavery cannot simply be brushed aside.
“He has said he is open to a formal state apology. But openness is not commitment. Until the government makes a full and unequivocal apology, that remains the obstacle to progress.”
She added: “Nobody is asking the average British person to take personal responsibility for enslavement. This is about the responsibility of the state. The British state protected and profited from enslavement.
“The British state compensated the slave owners, not the enslaved. And British taxpayers were still paying off that debt until 2015. States are held to their past actions all the time. This should be no different.”
Reports had suggested that the prime minister was open to increasing financial assistance for Commonwealth countries to help atone for Britain’s role.
But while Mr Burnham has said he is willing to consider an apology, both Downing Street and the Foreign Office (FCDO) denied he was looking at providing any extra financial assistance.
An FCDO spokesperson said: “We are committed to working with Commonwealth partners on issues facing the world, including the role of private finance in tackling global debt issues, addressing the climate crisis, and supporting economic development.”
A Downing Street source added that “the prime minister’s position is clear: we do not believe financial reparations for the slave trade is the right answer. We will not be making additional aid allocations on top of existing budgets.”
Later Downing Street denied that debt restructuring was related to slave reparations in a briefing with journalists.
A spokesman said: “The prime minister, like his predecessors, has expressed his sorrow and regret for the pain and suffering caused by the transatlantic slave trade, and recognized the way it still shapes our world today. That is distinct from a formal apology.
“We're opening a structured dialogue with those affected by the transatlantic slave trade and listening to calls for a formal apology on behalf of the British state, and that will form an important part of that process.
“We think it's right that a formal apology is discussed properly with the countries and communities most affected, rather than simply deciding unilaterally what form it should take.”
But the spokesman added: “Acknowledging the horror of the transatlantic slave trade and considering a formal apology for Britain's role in it does not mean accepting a present day financial liability.”
The row has come as Mr Burnham and King Charles attend the Commonwealth Heads of Government meeting in Antigua and Barbuda.
An event is being held alongside the CHOGM summit at the Trade Winds Hotel in Antigua entitled From Samoa to St John’s: Britain, the Commonwealth and the Road to Reparatory Justice.
Commonwealth leaders said Mr Burnham had made an “essential first step” towards a reparations deal, after he said he was open to making a formal apology for slavery.
Mia Mottley, the prime minister of Barbados, insisted that she expected “investment in health and education” and a “development partnership” with the UK.
Andrew Holness, the prime minister of Jamaica, called for “meaningful” discussions on “reparatory justice”.
Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has been critical of Mr Burnham’s willingness to make an apology, describing the reparations issue as a “distraction” and warning that the Commonwealth “needs to be forward-looking”.
Explaining why she opposes an apology, she told Sky News: “It’s because of what will happen next.
“What I’m worried about is that this CHOGM summit is yet another opportunity for people to start asking Britain for money because of the slave trade.”
Sir Michael Ellis, a former attorney-general, has warned: “An apology tantamount to accepting liability. If Burnham goes to an international conference and apologises, he is making it easier for those who want to take the UK to an international tribunal such as the UN, as they did with Chagos.”

articles.title_orig: Audemars Piguet Introduces Three Supersonnerie Watches And Two Stone-Dial Code 11.59 Models
articles.title_zh: Audemars Piguet Introduces Three Supersonnerie Watches And Two Stone-Dial Code 11.59 Models
articles.content_orig:
Audemars Piguet expands its Royal Oak and Code 11.59 collections with five new references that explore two very different aspects of the manufacture’s watchmaking. Three new Minute Repeater Supersonnerie models showcase its work in acoustic engineering, while two 38mm Code 11.59 Selfwinding watches introduce natural stone dials in gold obsidian and black onyx. The releases range from technically complex chiming watches to more restrained time-only models, with each offering a different interpretation of the collections’ long-standing designs.
The three minute repeaters share the same hand-wound caliber 2953 and Supersonnerie technology. Two arrive in the 42mm Royal Oak line, including the first pink gold version of this execution, while the third is a new iteration of the 41mm Code 11.59 Minute Repeater Supersonnerie. The two stone-dial watches, meanwhile, offer a more compact take on the Code 11.59, with cases in yellow or pink gold.
Audemars Piguet introduced its Supersonnerie technology in 2016 with the Royal Oak Concept RD#1. The result of eight years of development, the project brought together watchmakers, musicians, and researchers from the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Lausanne (EPFL). The objective was to improve the acoustic performance of a wristwatch minute repeater, a complication that presents particular challenges when producing a clear chime from a mechanism housed inside a relatively small case.
The patented construction uses gongs mounted on a dedicated soundboard. Combined with an innovative case construction and a newly developed regulator, this approach improves the striking mechanism’s acoustic performance. The latest watches use caliber 2953, a manually wound 30 × 6mm movement. It comprises 362 components and 32 jewels, operates at 3 Hz, and offers a minimum guaranteed power reserve of 72 hours. In addition to the minute repeater, the movement drives the hours, minutes, and small seconds.
The first of the new Royal Oak references, 26591TI.OO.1252TI.08 , features a 42mm titanium case and an integrated bracelet in the same material. Its green dial has a satin-finished sunburst motif and a smoked effect that darkens towards the edge. A matching green small-seconds counter maintains the color scheme, while 18K white gold Royal Oak hands and silver-toned 18K pink gold hour markers provide contrast. The indexes and central hands are filled with luminescent material.
As with other Royal Oak models, the case combines satin-brushed and polished surfaces. These alternating finishes create depth and detail across the watch’s angular architecture. The titanium reference measures 14 mm thick and is water-resistant to 20 meters.
The second Royal Oak Minute Repeater Supersonnerie, reference 26591OR.OO.1252OR.01 , offers a warmer interpretation. For the first time, Audemars Piguet presents this model in 18K pink gold, pairing the metal with a lovely brown Grande Tapisserie dial. The small-seconds counter follows the dial’s color, while the hands and lume-filled hour markers are also pink gold. A matching integrated bracelet completes the design. This watch shares the exact case dimensions and water resistance of its titanium counterpart.
The third watch brings Supersonnerie technology to the Code 11.59 collection. This 41mm reference 26395BC.OO.D009CR.01 is a new iteration of 2023’s Minute Repeater Supersonnerie. Its 18K white gold case features a fully polished middle, while the smoked sapphire dial reveals AP’s caliber 2953 beneath. The minute track and the rim around the small-seconds counter use galvanic growth to create additional texture and depth.
White gold baton hands and hour markers complete the display. The watch comes on a gray alligator strap with an 18K white gold folding clasp. With a 13.6mm profile, it is slightly slimmer than the two Royal Oak references, though it shares their 20m water resistance. All three watches have a price on request .
Alongside the minute repeaters, Audemars Piguet introduces two 38mm Code 11.59 Selfwinding models with natural stone dials. One uses gold obsidian, while the other features black onyx. Each material brings a different surface and character to the collection, with the finishing process intended to reveal the stone’s particular color, texture, and depth.
The yellow gold reference 77410BA.OO.A604CR.01 features a natural obsidian dial with a sunburst motif. Gold obsidian contains mineral inclusions that produce reflective details within its dark surface. The finish brings these variations into view, creating subtle changes as light moves across the dial. Yellow gold hands filled with luminescent material and gold-toned hour markers complement the case. A shimmering brown inner bezel and black alligator strap add further contrast.
The second model, reference 77410OR.OO.A001CR.01, combines an 18K pink gold case with a mirror-polished black onyx dial. The stone’s deep black surface provides a backdrop for baguette-cut diamond indexes, totaling 0.37 carats. Pink gold hands filled with luminescent material tie the dial to the case, while a black inner bezel and a shiny black alligator strap maintain the darker aesthetic.
Both watches measure 38 mm across and 9.6 mm thick. They feature double-curved, glare-proofed sapphire crystals on the front and back and offer water resistance to 30 meters. The yellow gold version retails for CHF 45,500 , while the pink gold one costs CHF 54,100 .
Inside, the automatic caliber 5909 provides hours, minutes, and a central seconds hand. This 26.2 × 3.9mm movement consists of 174 components, including 29 jewels, and runs at 4 Hz. Its minimum guaranteed power reserve is 60 hours.
These five additions highlight two notably different areas of Audemars Piguet’s watchmaking. The Supersonnerie references emphasize the engineering behind a complex chiming complication, presenting the same movement across two dissimilar collection designs and three material executions. The two smaller Code 11.59 models, meanwhile, use natural stone to create distinct dial designs within a time-only format. Together, the releases expand the Royal Oak and Code 11.59 collections through different approaches to materials, finishing, and mechanical watchmaking.
What do you think of these releases from Audemars Piguet? Let me know in the comments!

articles.title_orig: Spraying vinegar on your car windshield: what it’s for and why it’s recommended
articles.title_zh: Spraying vinegar on your car windshield: what it’s for and why it’s recommended
articles.content_orig:
TheCoolist is a mood board for your headspace.
Frosty mornings are back, and with them the ice scraper. On October 30, a Norwegian home site reported that drivers there swear by a kitchen staple sprayed on the glass the evening before, a tip El Cronista has also shared in English. It’s plain white vinegar. Here’s what it can really do, what it can’t, and where it can cause damage.
The method comes from the Norwegian site Houz.no : 3 parts white vinegar to 1 part cold or lukewarm water, with one or two drops of dish soap if you want it to spread more evenly. You spray it on a clean windshield in the evening, ideally when frost is forecast, then wipe it lightly with a microfiber cloth to spread the film without rubbing it off. In the morning, a couple of passes of the wipers clears the light dew.
The English edition of El Cronista adds that vinegar also cleans the glass, removing insect remains, tree sap and hard-water marks, and may reduce condensation inside the car. It attributes the anti-frost effect to the acetic acid lowering the freezing point of water, the way salt does.
Partly. The fact-checking site Snopes concludes that the mixture “may help prevent the glass from frosting” but “probably won’t help clear already iced-over glass,” and notes there is “no consensus” on how well it works. The VERIFY team at WUSA9 reached the same split verdict after checking with AAA: “once that ice is on there, spraying this mixture won’t remove it,” because its freezing point is “just barely lower than that of water.” As a preventive step, though, it “could work.”
Vinegar is an acid, so where it lands matters. Snopes advises wiping up any spills on paint or chrome promptly, and Houz.no recommends keeping the spray away from the wiper rubber, which it can dry out. Auto glass professionals quoted by VERIFY warn that extended exposure can make damage worse on a windshield that’s already chipped or cracked. In extreme cold, a thin layer of frost may still form, and the smell can be strong on the first drive, so crack a window. Whatever you do, never pour hot water on frozen glass: Houz.no points out that the thermal shock can crack it. Commercial frost-prevention sprays remain an alternative, Snopes notes.
White vinegar has other uses around the house, from dull, dirty keys to the floor around the toilet . And while you’re getting ready for winter, here’s what carpenters do to the deck before the first snow .
A spray bottle, a thin layer and a calm night. That’s the trick.

articles.title_orig: Goodbye to the toilet brush: the more hygienic alternative more and more bathrooms are switching to
articles.title_zh: Goodbye to the toilet brush: the more hygienic alternative more and more bathrooms are switching to
articles.content_orig:
TheCoolist is a mood board for your headspace.
It sits next to every toilet, usually in a closed holder, and a Finnish cleaning expert says many people keep it far too long. In Scandinavia and Central Europe, home sites report that many households are now swapping the classic bristle toilet brush for a different design. Here’s what is replacing it, why cleaning pros say it’s more hygienic, and what it still can’t do.
According to the Norwegian site Dagens.no , many people are choosing a silicone brush over the traditional plastic one. The reasons it gives: there are no dense bristles for dirt to collect in, so the head rinses clean; the flexible head reaches the edges and hard-to-access areas; it tends to spray less; and it is often sold with a ventilated or wall-mounted holder that lets it dry faster. The site quotes Finnish cleaning expert Mari Breilin, who says plastic brushes should be replaced considerably more often than many people do. The price, it adds, is about the same as many ordinary brushes.
The British testing site Expert Reviews sums it up: bristles are “so tightly packed together that it’s impossible to clean them perfectly,” so “bacteria build-up on the brush is inevitable,” and they “need replacing much more often.” Cleaning expert Isabella Flores, of Sparkly Maid San Diego, told Tom’s Guide that silicone is non-porous, so it doesn’t absorb bacteria and organic matter the way plastic bristles can. It also dries faster and tolerates harsher disinfection, including boiling.
Silicone or not, the routine is what keeps it hygienic. Tom’s Guide recommends:
Silicone is not a miracle. Expert Reviews notes that silicone brushes shaped like regular ones “usually have weak bristles that don’t do a great job on stubborn dirt,” and that flat, spatula-style heads handle grime better, though you have to get used to a different technique. And no brush, silicone or bristle, is built to dissolve the hard mineral ring at the waterline. And whatever you choose, a brush kept damp in a closed holder will still breed bacteria.
For that waterline ring, here’s the best way to remove limescale from the toilet . The bathroom is changing in other ways too, like the option replacing toilet paper , and the floor around the base deserves attention: see why people are spraying vinegar around the toilet .
A flat silicone head, an open holder and a date to replace it. That’s the trick.

articles.title_orig: Intel Stock Slides Again Monday: What's Going On? - Intel (NASDAQ:INTC)
articles.title_zh: Intel Stock Slides Again Monday: What's Going On? - Intel (NASDAQ:INTC)
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Shares of Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) have been in phenomenal form on the stock market since the beginning of 2025, rising by 225% as of this writing, but Chipzilla's investors received a huge shock after the release of its third-quarter 2026 results on Oct. 29.
Intel stock plunged more than 28% the following day. Investors were spooked by the company's guidance, which was affected by the poor performance of its personal computer (PC) business. However, a closer look at Intel's numbers and guidance suggests that the stock is only taking a breather.
Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »
Let's look at the reasons why this semiconductor stock could overcome this setback and soar once again.
Image source: Getty Images.
Intel's Q4 revenue increased 21% year over year to $16.5 billion. Even better, its non-GAAP earnings per share jumped by an incredible 126% from the year-ago period to $0.52. Wall Street would have settled for $0.40 in adjusted earnings per share on revenue of $16.5 billion, suggesting that Intel's bottom-line performance was well ahead of expectations.
However, the company's guidance led investors to press the panic button. The company expects revenue of $15-$16 billion in the current quarter, along with adjusted earnings per share of $0.25. Analysts were anticipating $0.43 in earnings per share on $17.1 billion in revenue. So, it is easy to see why Intel stock was hammered badly following its results.
The primary reason behind Intel's poor outlook is the PC business. The company's client computing and physical artificial intelligence (AI) business segment saw revenue drop 5% from the year-ago period to $8.1 billion. Intel management noted on the earnings call that the pace of the PC market slowdown has accelerated over the past couple of months, driven by high component costs that are weighing on IT budgets.
Intel noted that it expects "the current environment to persist until memory availability and prices begin to normalize." This statement indicates that Intel's client computing business faces sustained pressure, especially given its expectation that the PC market will shrink by 10% in 2027. However, Intel's data center business is more than making up for the decline in PCs.
Its data center and AI (DCAI) segment revenue jumped 78% year over year to $7.3 billion, driven by solid demand for its server central processing units (CPUs) that handle inference and agentic AI workloads in data centers. Importantly, Intel's server CPUs are gaining popularity among customers, with Oracle deciding to deploy its next-generation Diamond Rapids platform to power its cloud infrastructure.
At the same time, Intel's custom AI processor business is also gaining solid traction. The company noted that this is its "fastest growing business segment, tripling over the last 3 years and poised to triple again over the next few years." As such, there is a strong chance that the robust performance of the DCAI business will enable Intel to offset the weakness of the PC segment until the latter stabilizes.
Market research firm IDC expects the PC market to start growing again from 2028, so the pain Intel is facing in this segment may not last beyond next year. Additionally, Intel notes that it expects stronger demand from data center customers and that the market for data center chips will remain tight on supply in both 2027 and 2028.
This should help Intel deliver strong earnings growth on the back of favorable pricing. In fact, the company's earnings are expected to jump once again in the current quarter despite the challenging PC environment. The midpoint of its Q4 revenue guidance implies a 13% jump from the year-ago period, along with an impressive 67% increase in earnings per share.
So, Intel continues to clock impressive earnings growth even though it isn't firing on all cylinders. Once the PC market starts recovering from 2028, I won't be surprised to see Intel's growth accelerating further.
If you're looking to construct a million-dollar portfolio and want to buy a top growth stock trading at an attractive valuation right now, Intel seems like an ideal candidate. That's because Intel trades at an attractive 31 times forward earnings, which isn't very expensive considering that the iShares Semiconductor ETF , which tracks the semiconductor sector, has a price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 46.
Moreover, analysts expect Intel's earnings growth to continue at a solid pace.
INTC EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts
Even better, the long-term earnings-per-share growth estimates for Intel are a handsome 75%.
INTC EPS LT Growth Estimates data by YCharts
As such, there is a strong likelihood that this AI stock will regain its mojo. Let's say Intel's earnings per share reach $3.14 in 2028 (based on YCharts estimates), and it trades at 40 times earnings; its stock price could jump to $126. That's 90% higher than Intel's price right now, suggesting that this beaten-down chipmaker could almost double in just over two years.
So, the recent slide in Intel seems like a golden opportunity for investors to buy a top stock that could make them significantly richer.

articles.title_orig: Fake alerts warn of nuclear danger as Ukraine and Russia report emergency app hacks
articles.title_zh: Fake alerts warn of nuclear danger as Ukraine and Russia report emergency app hacks
articles.content_orig:
Nuclear danger, radiation threat and street combat: Ukrainians received a wave of messages Sunday night that raised alarm with a series of grave — and baseless — warnings.
Authorities said the country’s emergency alert application had been targeted in a cyberattack, and hours later Russia said its own alert system had also been hacked. The dueling accusations came just as a rare humanitarian ceasefire between the two sides ended, raising fears of intensified fighting rather than a move toward broader peace.
Residents in Ukraine have become used to the unsettling alerts that buzz their phones with news of incoming Russian missiles and drones — a service millions rely on to seek shelter before the attacks hit their cities. But the warnings Sunday night immediately stood out.
The messages, which began around 10:45 p.m. Kyiv time (3:45 p.m. ET), warned residents not to go outside because of  radiation hazard, chemical threat and street fights.
Another message professed, in Russian, that all of Ukraine was under nuclear alert. “Don’t worry,” it added. “Oreshnik is in action,” referring to Russia’s nuclear-capable hypersonic missile.
That message referenced a Telegram channel called Hitcorecorp. Major pro-Kremlin Telegram channel Mash said it spoke with the group and that it took responsibility for the hack. NBC News could not verify who the group is and whether it was responsible for the alerts.
Shortly after the alerts went out late Sunday, Ukraine’s air force said the country’s “Air Alert” app had likely been “compromised by the enemy,” confirming there was no “radiation threat” and urging calm.
In separate statements, the app’s creators said “unauthorized third parties interfered with the operation of the app,” forcing them to temporarily suspend its operations. It later called the incident a “cyberattack,” saying it was gradually restoring the service. “The team is carrying out additional measures to protect the app in order to prevent similar situations in the future,” one of the statements said.
Ukrainian media reported that users across the country received the alert, and authorities in the western Lviv region reported that some of the public warning sirens and loudspeaker systems broadcast a “radiation hazard” signal.
Still, many Ukrainians did not appear unduly alarmed or panicked by the alerts. In fact, many shared memes online, poking fun at what they saw as a blatant fake, and the fact the warning was issued in Russian. “No one was particularly surprised,” one user wrote on X. “They might as well have thrown in a dinosaur attack, too.”
Russian drone strikes in Ukraine kill two teenage girls
The state emergency service of Ukraine said Monday the national alert system was operating normally, and an NBC News producer in Kyiv did not experience any further issues with the “Air Alert” app.
Meanwhile, Russia’s emergencies ministry also said early Monday that its mobile application has suffered a “massive cyberattack,” resulting in what it said was “dissemination of fake information to the public.” The public alert system was restored and was operating normally, it said shortly after. It emphasized that the app was only “an additional, supplementary information service.”
Screenshots shared by Russian media and some regional authorities suggested the alert, issued in Russian, warned of “nuclear warheads” launched at Russia. As with the Ukrainian alert, the wording was casual and did not appear official.
Russian authorities did not say who was to blame for the alleged cyberattack, only saying “malicious actors” were behind it.
It was not immediately clear whether the two incidents were linked.
It came just hours after a temporary ceasefire between Kyiv and Moscow came to an end in the occupied southern Ukrainian region of Kherson.
The truce, brokered with involvement from first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV, held without violations from either side for six days, allowing the evacuation of hundreds of residents from the frontline town of Oleshky , which had been on the brink of a humanitarian catastrophe.
The truce amounted to the biggest de-escalation between Kyiv and Moscow since the war started in early 2022.
“On behalf of America, I commend Russia and Ukraine for their leadership and cooperation surrounding the Oleshky ceasefire,” Melania Trump said in a post on X on Sunday. “I hope Oleshky serves as a foundation for lasting peace between both nations.”
Ukraine’s ombudsman ​for human rights, Dmytro Lubinets, said he was exploring opportunities for “further humanitarian initiatives” with his Russian counterpart, Yana Lantratova, adding that it was “important to maintain this mechanism of cooperation.”
Before the truce took hold, the United Nations estimated that some 2,000 civilians remained in Oleshky, many experiencing hunger and unable to leave safely because of heavily mined roads.
Neither side has disclosed the exact number of people evacuated, but the first lady said Sunday it was nearly 800. The evacuees could go into territory controlled by either Ukraine or Russia, or remain in the town, officials on both sides said.
Lantratova, the Russian human rights commissioner, said Monday that she had expected more people to evacuate from Oleshky, saying “quite a few empty buses” left the area. Many people chose to stay because they couldn’t leave elderly or sick loved ones, she said, or simply refused to leave their homes no matter what.
She said for those remaining, humanitarian aid deliveries would take place at least monthly, with the “coordination and mediation” of Melania Trump.
Ukraine’s armed forces accused Russia on Monday of using the truce to rotate its units and fortify positions in the area. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Kyiv also could have used the ceasefire to regroup, calling it a “completely common practice in such situations.”
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.

articles.title_orig: Python struggles to escape as more than 10 mongooses bite and tug to defend one of their own
articles.title_zh: Python struggles to escape as more than 10 mongooses bite and tug to defend one of their own
articles.content_orig:
A python that appeared to grab a mongoose soon faced an unexpected barrage of more than 12 members of the small mammal's group fighting back.
The video , shared on Instagram by Bestial Nature (@bestialnature) starts with the attack underway. It appears that the python has one mongoose wrapped tightly in its grip, while at least a dozen furry friends and family members assault the snake from every angle.
A colony or pack can offer a mongoose protection. Members may confront a threat together when one of them is endangered. This form of defense occurs in some social species of these small, carnivorous mammals.
The snake eventually lunges at other mongooses, but the horde appears to be too much for the serpent to handle. The video ends before there is a conclusion, but the mongoose clan seems to be overwhelming the snake, so it's hard to imagine it ends well for the reptile.
Several details about the encounter remain unclear. The account does not identify either species, provide a location, or establish what ultimately happened to the animals.
Mammals, birds, and reptiles are usual python prey, with the mix depending on the snake's species and size. A mongoose is not a staple food, but pythons may take the opportunity to eat one, according to A-Z Animals.
A python applies pressure by coiling around an animal after first taking hold with its teeth. Pythons, unlike cobras, are nonvenomous. A python's species matters when considering its length. Some species grow to just a few feet long, while the largest can exceed 20 feet.
Forests, grasslands, rocky terrain, savannas, scrublands, and open woodlands all provide mongoose habitat, though species use them differently. These mammals occur mainly in Africa and Asia.
Pythons, meanwhile, live in forests, wetlands, rocky areas, grasslands, and scrublands, creating some overlap with mongoose habitats. The snakes' range covers Africa and Asia and extends to Australia and parts of Oceania.
Resistance to venom does not prevent a python from constricting a mongoose. According to A-Z Animals, some mongoose species resist particular neurotoxins, especially those in cobra venom. In encounters with snakes, mongooses also depend on agility and quick bites.
A venomous bite can still endanger a mongoose despite its resistance to certain venoms. According to A-Z Animals, that resistance in some mongooses comes from alterations to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors that make them less susceptible to those toxins.
These related stories involve pythons swallowing prey, a cobra-python standoff, and a snake lunging at handlers.
• Near an airport in Maharashtra, a 10-foot python turned a rescue into a tug-of-war.
• In Rajasthan, a python swallowed a jackal and became trapped in a farm fence.
• In Assam, villagers returned a python to the wild after it swallowed six ducks.
• A Bihar family fled as a king cobra and python squared off.
• In South Africa, a snake lunged at handlers as a narrator warned it was upset.

articles.title_orig: Fake nuclear warnings issued after Ukrainian and Russian air alert apps hacked
articles.title_zh: Fake nuclear warnings issued after Ukrainian and Russian air alert apps hacked
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine and Russia have both said air alert apps were hacked on Sunday night after fake messages warning of attacks, including nuclear, were sent to users.
Ukraine's widely used app sent red-level air raid warnings across the country, with additional warnings of radiation, chemical attacks, and street fighting sent to some residents in areas including Kyiv.
A few hours later, Russian authorities said a similar app was hacked after fake alerts, some of which contained foul language, were triggered.
It was unclear who was behind the cyberattacks or whether the two incidents were connected.
Many Ukrainian citizens are used to receiving almost nightly alerts warning of incoming Russian missile and drone attacks. Some told the BBC that, four and a half years into the war, they have disabled the app altogether.
After Sunday night's hack, the country's air force urged people to consult other official channels.
In a post on Telegram, the air force said: "The Air Alarm application has probably been subjected to hostile interference. There is no radiation threat! Stay calm and follow our updates on our [Telegram] channel."
The government said it had temporarily disabled the app for maintenance, saying it had "apparently been compromised".
Some of the fake warnings were written in Russian, which would have alerted many users to the fact they were not legitimate.
But Olena, a Kyiv resident, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme she had been alarmed, saying: "The first thought was 'oh my god, I'm not prepared for this'.
"I'm prepared for blackouts, for a cut in central heating and water supply, but not for nuclear attack."
Olena says her husband then received alerts for "street fighting attacks in Kyiv" and another alert, written in Russian.
"After that I understood that somebody had attacked the app, because all notifications we get in Ukrainian."
In Russia, the government said one of its air raid alert apps had also been targeted by "a massive cyberattack", which sent "fake information to the public".
A purported screenshot of a fake alert was shared on Telegram by Atesh, a partisan Ukrainian group operating inside Russian-held territory.
It warned some users that "nuclear warheads mounted on P1-Suns [a Ukrainian attack drone] had been launched at all regions of Russia".
The alert, which included profanities, opened with a message telling residents there was a "risk of [things] getting lively" and told them to "stock up urgently on food for three weeks and hide".
On Monday morning there was no sense the messages had caused widespread panic in Russia and the incident did not feature prominently on media outlets.
Asked about the breach, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov did not address it specifically but said all Russian government internet resources were "one way or another... under constant cyberattacks", including the presidential site, which is targeted "round the clock".
He said the proliferation of AI technology was contributing to an increase in cyberattacks.
Russia's emergencies ministry said on Monday that the app's "full functionality will be restored by the end of the day" and the hack had not impacted the wider alert system.
While both Russia and Ukraine are widely believed to carry out cyberattacks against one another, the informal language used in the hoax alerts on Sunday pointed to so-called hacktivist groups, which could be aligned to Moscow or Kyiv but are not formally directed by either government.
Those responsible for the hack on Russia's system have likely had the capability to launch such an attack for some time but decided to hold off until Ukraine's alert app was compromised, cyber experts told the BBC.
Oleksander Merezhko, chair of the foreign affairs committee in the Ukrainian parliament, said the attack did not cause panic or extreme reactions.
Merezhko told the BBC that Ukrainians, especially in Kyiv, were used to "practically non-stop alerts", adding "this message was in Russian language which immediately aroused suspicions".
He continued: "It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that. It is possible and we are quite prepared for such possibilities."
Herbert Lin, a senior research scholar for cyber policy and security at Stanford University, told BBC World Service's Newsday programme: "I think it's the first time [a hack of this kind] happened to an official Ukrainian information app, but I suspect it won't be the last."
The alerts in Ukraine were sent minutes before the end of a localised ceasefire in Ukraine's frontline Kherson region, which was implemented last Tuesday. It had been brokered in part by US First Lady Melania Trump to allow civilians to evacuate the Russian-occupied city of Oleshky.
Fighting continued elsewhere while the Kherson ceasefire was in place. In the city of Dnipro alone, 15 people were killed in an attack on a train platform on Thursday.
Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Additional reporting by Jamie Whitehead and Helen Davidson

articles.title_orig: Trump's Iran threat renews Gulf fears of a war it didn't choose
articles.title_zh: Trump's Iran threat renews Gulf fears of a war it didn't choose
articles.content_orig:
Third day of indirect talks as Qatar tries to negotiate release of $6bn in Iranian assets that could lead to waterway’s reopening
Officials from the Gulf states are “braced for the worst” as they wait for Washington’s response to an Iranian proposal that could reopen the strait of Hormuz before the US midterm elections on Tuesday.
Indirect talks in Doha ran into a third day on Sunday with Qatar trying to negotiate the release of more than $6bn in Iranian assets, which could lead to the reopening of the strait of Hormuz and the restart of negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme.
The United Arab Emirates envoy Anwar Gargash said another round of escalation was not in the interests of Iran or any of its neighbours. He said: “We are also, as we have shown before, braced for the worst.”
He added: “Relations with Iran are essential, because Iran is our neighbour and we do not want to see it get caught up in a prolonged crisis.”
Qatar’s mediation continued despite unidentified missiles striking a Pakistan-bound Qatari LNG tanker near the strait of Hormuz on Friday. The attack came despite the ship receiving direct clearance and safe-passage approval from Tehran just hours earlier.
In a bid to overcome the lack of trust on both sides, Qatar has been focusing its efforts on reaching an agreement for a plan to compress the process by which the US lifts sanctions and then Iran reopens the strait of Hormuz and starts nuclear talks. Iran has agreed to cut the timetable from seven to two days.
Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said he hoped the US would choose “diplomacy over other paths”. He said Iran was ready for both defence and diplomacy, depending on Washington’s “rationality”. Araghchi said there were currently no plans for direct talks with Washington.
Araghchi has not been attending the mediation in Doha and is due to go to Turkmenistan on Monday, but other Iranian diplomats are heavily involved.
Donald Trump said on Saturday the US had knocked out much of Iran’s military but still had to “take care of” one or two targets, as Tehran warned of reprisals if attacked. He maintained that negotiations with Iran to end the war, started by the US and Israel in February, were “going fine but you know they’re not very reliable”.
Earlier on Saturday, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the US was open to a diplomatic solution, while Iran’s security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, disclosed that he had received a letter from the US vice-president, JD Vance, seeking to revive talks.
Rezaei noted what he described as a positive change in “tone” from the US side but said he had yet to respond.
Speaking to Al Jazeera on Saturday, Araghchi said Iran had offered to open the strait of Hormuz within two days of the US acting to lift the blockade on oil ships, stop blocking the release of Iranian assets and end sanctions on Iranian oil exports.
Ali Nikzad, the deputy speaker of Iran’s parliament, once again signalled that Tehran would be unwilling to discuss its nuclear programme, saying: “Our enemies must understand that the Iranian nation has made a decision not to negotiate on the nuclear issue under any circumstances or under any pressure. This great nation gave its enemies enough opportunity to negotiate in this area, but was faced with repeated breaches of promises and illegal bombing of part of peaceful nuclear facilities.”
Rezaei claimed Trump was being hounded by a war that he claimed was having wider international repercussions than the Vietnam war. He told Iranian TV on Saturday: “Today, wherever Trump goes, he must answer why he started the war against Iran. There is no family in America that has not endured the pressure caused by the war in Iran.”

articles.title_orig: Why investors are dumping tech stocks, in one image
articles.title_zh: Why investors are dumping tech stocks, in one image
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Tech stocks aren't getting shredded for any old reason. It's actually very fundamental: Free cash flow is drying up for Big Tech leaders, and capex is rising dramatically.
Investors are questioning whether this ratio is totally out of whack, given more realistic growth projections for AI.
The combined capex of Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Microsoft rose by $36.9 billion in the third quarter to $201.9 billion, the team at The Kobeissi Letter calculated (chart below). This figure has more than doubled over the past 12 months, and is up a staggering 356% since the first quarter of 2024.
Big Tech has now spent $1.6 trillion on capex over the last three years, the strategists say. At the same time, the combined free cash flow of these companies fell $33.1 billion last quarter to a negative $26.4 billion, its lowest on record. Free cash flow among these tech beasts has fallen by $88.2 billion over the last year. Only Microsoft reported positive free cash flow in the third quarter. Looking ahead, the strategists estimate these four companies plan to spend another $232 billion on capex in the fourth quarter.
The AI trade saw a serious slamming on Friday, with more than $1 trillion in market value wiped away as investors fretted about the weakening cash flow profiles of Big Tech.
"The AI narrative is cracking as profitability concerns intensify," warned Miller Tabak chief markets strategist Matt Maley.

Alongside an overhaul of Google Messages’ settings , Google appears to be preparing a fresh coat of paint for the app icon of its default texting app. The latest Google beta comes with a new Google Messages icon, complete with the newer gradient look that aligns it better with other recently redesigned Google icons .
The current Google Messages icon relies on a flat, minimalist aesthetic: two interlocking horizontal pill shapes in contrasting shades of blue, forming a third overlapping tone in the center. It is clean and modern, but distinctly abstract and screams “messaging app” in the right way. You can see it in the image above.
The latest Google Messages v20261030 beta comes with this new gradient icon out of the box:
The new design shifts toward a more expressive depiction of a messaging conversation bubble. Instead of the flat pills, the foreground features a plump, rounded speech bubble. It also incorporates a smooth gradient, blending from a softer pinkish-blue highlight across the top edge down into a vibrant royal blue. Tucked behind it to the upper-left is a darker solid blue bubble, carrying over some inspiration from the previous icon and depicting an ongoing conversation.
The new Google Messages icon is also available on Wear OS with the same beta version of Google Messages:
The icon is available to beta users. It remains to be seen if this is the finalized design and when Google will roll it out to the stable branch.

articles.title_orig: Record reward offered for capture of fugitive cocaine kingpin dubbed "Chubby Jos"
articles.title_zh: Record reward offered for capture of fugitive cocaine kingpin dubbed "Chubby Jos"
articles.content_orig:
Dutch authorities are offering a record reward of 2 million euros ($2.2 million) for information leading to the arrest of Jos Leijdekkers , one of Europe's most-wanted drug traffickers, currently hiding in Sierra Leone.
The arrest of Leijdekkers, also known as "Bolle Jos" ("Chubby Jos"), is "the highest priority for the Public Prosecution Service and the police," said Dutch prosecutors in a statement, multiplying by 10 their previous reward.
Leijdekkers is considered to be one of the key players in the international cocaine trade.
A court in Rotterdam sentenced him in absentia in 2024 to 24 years in prison for drug shipments totaling nearly 7,000 kilos of cocaine, an armed robbery, and ordering a "liquidation."
He has also been sentenced to 79 years in prison in Belgium.
Dutch police have tracked the 35-year-old to Sierra Leone. Any information shared with prosecutors will be kept secret, the Dutch authorities said in a statement.
Justice Minister David van Weel said the increase in the reward was "necessary given the threat that Leijdekkers poses to national security, our democratic rule of law, and the international legal order."
"The Netherlands, in cooperation with the international community, is doing everything in its power to secure the arrest of Leijdekkers," the minister said in a letter to parliament.
In January 2025, Dutch authorities said they were "absolutely certain" he was hiding out in Sierra Leone. The BBC reported that Dutch prosecutor Wim de Bruin said the fugitive's return to the Netherlands was of "the highest priority."
Images apparently showing Leijdekkers in the company of officials as high as President Julius Maada Bio have sparked speculation that the cocaine baron has cozied up to Sierra Leone's political class — including the president's daughter.
Suspicions that he was in Sierra Leone arose after the country's first lady, Fatima Bio, posted pictures and a video on social media that showed a man strongly resembling Leijdekkers at a religious service, also attended by President Bio.
Leijdekkers is also believed to be involved in the disappearance and death of Naima Jillal, a woman who went missing in 2019 after she got into a car in Amsterdam, according to Europol . Intercepted messages allegedly showed that Leijdekkers "played an important role in Jillal's disappearance," the agency said.
"For a long time, there was no trace of Naima Jillal, until photos of a woman believed to be her were found on a phone seized in the Marengo investigation," Europol said. "The photos show that she was most likely tortured and is probably no longer alive."

articles.title_orig: Dell XPS Googlebook Review: Beautiful Hardware For A Useless Platform
articles.title_zh: Dell XPS Googlebook Review: Beautiful Hardware For A Useless Platform
articles.content_orig:
Googlebook OS still needs a ton of work.
I can think of a few reasons to buy a Googlebook , but they're all pretty dystopian. Maybe every other computing platform has succumbed to a super AI-powered virus, leaving a Googlebook as your only option. Or perhaps Google has taken over the world and has started hunting down people who use Windows, Linux or macOS. In a world where a Googlebook is your only option, then the $1,000 Dell XPS Googlebook is probably the one to get. But in the real world, where you can get the exact same XPS hardware running on more flexible platforms with better developer support, the XPS Googlebook seems practically pointless.
But let's back up a bit and talk about Googlebook OS, Google's new laptop platform that's a combination of both Android and ChromeOS. It supports Android apps natively, it can synchronize and mirror apps from your Android phone, and it has Google's Gemini AI integrated throughout its interface. Technically, Googlebook OS should be an upgrade from ChromeOS, a platform built entirely around Google's web browser. But, after testing this laptop for the last week, I'd go so far as to say the entire Googlebook concept is a failure.
Who really wants a laptop running unoptimized Android apps? Why buy into an untested Google platform just to synchronize your Android phone, especially when you can mirror and sync Android device texts on Windows and Linux? And why would you pay the same exact price as a Windows PC for a computer that does so much less? While Apple, Microsoft and PC makers are sweating to push the computing industry forward this year, most notably with the launch of NVIDIA's RTX Spark and Apple's redesigned touchscreen MacBook Pro , Google has given us a new platform that is in many ways less useful than its aging Chromebooks.
For its first (and I'm hoping only) Googlebook, Dell took its recent XPS 13 design and refashioned it for Google's new OS. It still has a slim 2.2-pound metal case, making it one of the lightest systems in this size range, and it sports a 13.4-inch InfinityEdge screen. It's powered by a Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite chip with 16GB of RAM — the same hardware on the $1,000 Windows 11 XPS 13. There are only two USB-C ports on either side of the XPS 13 Googlebook, and, unfortunately, there's no headphone jack.
A multi-colored "Glowbar" occasionally lights up on the rear of the XPS 13 — something that Google highlights as one of the defining features of Googlebook OS — but it's ultimately superfluous. It can show your charging status and battery level, but it's not exactly solving any major problems for laptop users.
It's not unusual to see PC makers reusing their designs — many companies are also recycling their existing work for NVIDIA's RTX Spark chip. But at least that platform has a few halo products designed specifically for it, like the Surface Laptop Ultra. There's nothing highlighting what's truly special about Googlebook OS — arguably because there's not exactly much to show off.
I could tell you that the XPS Googlebook has a very nice screen, a comfortable keyboard and a very accurate touchpad. I could tell you that its slim design and light weight makes it easy to tote around without weighing down your bag. But really, you could have learned all of that from my review of the standard XPS 13 with Windows 11. Everything good about this system comes from Dell's excellent design work.
Once I started using Googlebook OS, though, it became instantly clear that Googlebook OS is simply a hot mess. It's fine for web browsing with Chrome and accessing Google apps like Gmail and Calendar, but support for Android apps via the Google Play store is mostly disappointing. Slack only works as a mobile Android app, allowing you to see a single channel or direct message, but there's no wider desktop view like you'd see on Windows or macOS. You also can't easily react to messages and images in Slack — instead, you have to perform a long click, as you would on a normal Android phone. Evernote, meanwhile, doesn't appear at all on the Googlebook Play Store. (And yes, I still use Evernote a ton. There are dozens of us!)
"Desktop optimized" Android apps function more like you'd expect on other laptop platforms. Notability, CapCut Pad and Luminar all offer more fully-featured apps for taking AI notes and editing media, but they're only useful if those apps are already part of your workflow. I can't imagine too many people will change their editing process just to find something compatible with Googlebook OS.
Using the XPS Googlebook for my typical workflow often felt like pulling teeth. While Chrome worked fine for web browsing, resizing a photo required an odyssey through several different apps until I stumbled into Pixlr, a desktop-optimized editing app that only lets you resize an image when exporting it. Adobe Lightroom only seemed to let me resize a picture by cropping it (and it also kept bugging me to subscribe to Lightroom Premium to unlock more editing features). I eventually discovered that the standalone Viewer app has an easy way to resize images, something that isn't present in the default Photos app.
With no support for Audacity, I had to use Lexis Audio Editor to make some tweaks to a podcast file, but its basic interface seemed unsuited to more complicated edits. I might as well have just used an online editor like Audiomass (which, by the way, works just fine on Chromebooks). I also had to rely on Evernote's website to write this review, which required logging in every single time I turned on the XPS Googlebook, because the Evernote Android app was unavailable. I also eventually gave up on the Slack Android app and started using its web interface, which at least let me see all of my channels and direct messages.
I'm used to computers being gateways to sophisticated software and healthy developer support. Using the XPS Googlebook felt like being trapped in a computing stripmall: It's hobbled together by a variety of small apps of varying quality. Thank goodness for web apps, at least.
It's worth noting that Chromebooks also supported Android apps, so I don't believe there was actually a huge demand for a new Android-based computing platform.
I also wasn't impressed by any of the other Googlebook features: Syncing your Android phone to a Googlebook sounds nice in theory, but in reality it leads to redundant notifications if you have the same apps installed on both systems. You can also mirror an Android app from your phone — but again, why would you do that when you can run the app directly on the Googlebook? Given that you can already mirror Android phones and synchronize texts on Windows computers, I'm not sure why anyone would jump into a whole new platform just for these features.
Google being Google, of course, the company also crammed in as many Gemini AI features as it could into this platform. You can ask questions or edit media on the Gemini app, or wiggle the mouse pointer to ask the AI about things you encounter on the web or inside of apps. Gemini did a decent job of answering questions about products that we've featured on Engadget, but unless you absolutely want to lean on Google's AI, there really is no reason to buy a whole laptop just to have Gemini baked into everything.
Google's Rambler AI dictation feature, which lets you dictate text by speaking naturally, is also built into Googlebook OS, and from my testing it seemed to work pretty well. But it doesn't show you the text as you're speaking — it just shows a moving purple waveform, and that sometimes makes it hard to gather your thoughts or see what you were previously thinking. This is a big downside compared to just typing or using old-school dictation that used to be available on Android, but at least Rambler did a good job of cutting out natural "ums" and "uhhs," and it also formatted the text pretty well.
Battery life is another sign that the Googlebook OS platform is very unrefined. In the PCMark Android

articles.title_orig: China polysilicon prices hold amid market standoff, spot-futures gap
articles.title_zh: China polysilicon prices hold amid market standoff, spot-futures gap
articles.content_orig:
The China Mono Premium, the OPIS assessment for mono-grade polysilicon used in n-type ingot production, was unchanged at CNY 38.786 ($5.82)/kg, or CNY 0.081/W, according to the OPIS Global Solar Markets Report released on Oct. 27.
According to market participants, the fundamentals of the Chinese polysilicon market remain unchanged, with the market continuing to be characterized by manufacturers holding firm to full-cost-based offers while downstream buyers show limited willingness to accept current prices. This has kept prices largely at a standstill, with inventory levels exceeding 500,000 metric tons (MT) further prolonging the impasse.
Industry participants widely noted that futures prices, which remain significantly below mainstream spot prices, have provided a degree of balance to the ongoing standoff between upstream suppliers and downstream buyers. According to data from the Guangzhou Futures Exchange on Oct. 26, settlement prices for polysilicon futures contracts for delivery between November 2026 and October 2027 ranged from a low of CNY 33.620/kg to a high of CNY 37.180/kg, with even the highest about 4.14% below the latest spot assessment.
Market participants explained that actual spot transactions continue to be concluded at higher prices than futures contracts, partly because customers with long-term purchase agreements still need to procure some material in the spot market. To offset the higher procurement costs, these buyers also source relatively lower-priced polysilicon from futures traders, helping to balance their overall purchasing costs.
One trade participant said that futures traders had been gradually selling off previously accumulated stocks of low-priced polysilicon into the spot market. However, the availability of this lower-priced material is expected to diminish over time. The participant added that manufacturers adhering to the industry self-discipline agreement appear determined not to sell polysilicon at prices below CNY 40/kg during the fourth quarter. As low-priced supplies dwindle and manufacturers maintain their price stance, futures prices are expected to gradually rise, allowing actual spot transaction prices to find a new balance between futures prices and prevailing spot offers.
Separately, an industry source said the China Photovoltaic Industry Association would organize monitoring activities to oversee the implementation of polysilicon production cuts planned for the fourth quarter, adding that this gives the market a degree of confidence and expectation that prices will remain stable. However, no official confirmation or disclosure regarding these activities was available at the time of reporting.
Looking ahead, an upstream participant expected mainstream polysilicon offers to remain unchanged until the Lunar New Year in early February 2027. Meanwhile, prices offered by manufacturers that have not signed the pricing self-discipline agreement, along with polysilicon futures prices, are expected to remain below mainstream spot offers.
The Global Polysilicon Marker (GPM), the benchmark for polysilicon produced outside China, was assessed at $19.234/kg, or $0.040/W, unchanged from the previous week.
Both manufacturers and buyers in the global polysilicon market continued to face mounting pressure. One trade participant noted that some suppliers had reduced their China-based polysilicon sales teams to just a handful of people, underscoring the increasingly weak demand environment.
On the demand side, a source at an integrated manufacturer said that certain long-term contract holders with cell manufacturing facilities in the U.S. could still absorb around 300 MT of global polysilicon per month. While this volume provides some support for demand, the contribution remains relatively small and limited in scope.
Certain long-term contract holders, despite being in poor financial condition, reportedly continue to purchase global polysilicon at a loss due to their contractual obligations. However, the pricing mechanisms embedded in long-term contracts negotiated several years ago have given buyers some room to negotiate, potentially allowing these agreements to remain in effect despite challenging market conditions.
In the near term, industry participants generally expect the main sources of global polysilicon supply to remain U.S.-produced material and lower-priced polysilicon from other origins. In addition, the framework established under the Section 232 outcome has enabled limited volumes of compliant Chinese polysilicon to continue flowing into Southeast Asia.

articles.title_orig: PlayStation Is Engaging in a “Firmware War” Against Jailbreakers, as Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto VI Minimum Firmware Requirement Has Reportedly Changed
articles.title_zh: PlayStation Is Engaging in a “Firmware War” Against Jailbreakers, as Rockstar Games’ Grand Theft Auto VI Minimum Firmware Requirement Has Reportedly Changed
articles.content_orig:
Over the past few weeks, the hacking scene for current-generation gaming systems has made significant strides thanks to the advancement of AI models. While console jailbreaking is normally a significant issue that console manufacturers try to resolve as quickly as possible, Sony has an additional reason to act as quickly as possible, as it cannot afford to leave any hole unpatched on PlayStation 5 due to the release of Rockstar Games ' Grand Theft Auto VI .
A month after the 14.10.00 PlayStation 5 system software update, the 14.22.00.00 update has gone live today. This minor update introduces some “security fixes to the system software,” so there's little doubt that this update is the new move in the firmware war Sony engaged with jailbreakers.
What makes the release of this new PlayStation 5 system software update more interesting is how it is reportedly strictly related to Grand Theft Auto VI 's launch on November 19 . According to PlayStation Game Size , which tracks updates on the PlayStation Network database, the next entry in the Rockstar Games ' series will now require firmware 14.22.00 instead of 14.10.00 , which is unprecedented.
However, extreme situations call for extreme measures. With Grand Theft Auto VI set to sell the most on PlayStation 5 , Sony cannot allow any opening to piracy, as in the age of AI , even the smallest software vulnerability could have big consequences. And piracy could be only one of the consequences, as the game could be emulated and even recompiled into a native PC port before its official release , which would be disastrous for both Sony and Rockstar Games .
As jailbreakers and hackers will hardly stand down just because Sony is releasing multiple PlayStation 5 firmware updates in rapid succession, I expect this confrontation to continue even past November 19 , when Grand Theft Auto VI releases. Hopefully, things are not taken to an extreme that would lead to real consequences for paying customers.
About the author : Francesco De Meo has been covering video games and technology since 2012, starting his career at small outlets like Gamersyndrome and GeekSnack. 

After joining Wccftech gaming section in 2015, he quickly expanded his video gaming coverage with in-depth reporting, interviews with iconic industry figures such as Grasshopper Manufacture founder and No More Heroes creator Goichi "Suda51" Suda, Resident Evil series creator Shinji Mikami, Team NINJA's president and Nioh series director Fumihiko Yasuda, and Silent Hill creator Keiichiro Toyama, reviews and on-the-ground coverage of major industry events such as Gamescom and E3.

When he's not reporting or reviewing, Francesco can be found playing the genres he loves most, spending time with his six cats, reading, writing music, playing guitar and drumming for his progressive rock band.

articles.title_orig: European supermarkets hit by new fridge cyber attack
articles.title_zh: European supermarkets hit by new fridge cyber attack
articles.content_orig:
Chains in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg say fridge temperatures rose overnight, similar to hack of French stores
Supermarket chains in Sweden, Belgium and Luxembourg have said the temperatures of their refrigerators and freezers in dozens of stores rose overnight, prompting fears of a cyber-attack similar to one that caused millions of euros of food losses in France.
Sweden’s Coop chain told the daily Aftonbladet on Monday that six of ​its stores ‌had been ​affected, while ICA said it was “aware that a limited ​number of stores were affected by an incident overnight which impacted their refrigeration and freezer systems”.
The Dutch retailer Ahold Delhaize, which last ​month ​reported a ​cybersecurity ‌incident ​to police in the Netherlands, said an “IT incident” ​had hit fridges and ⁠freezers in dozens of its ⁠supermarkets in ​Belgium ‌and ‌Luxembourg.
A company spokesperson, Sarah ‌De Meester, said the supermarket chain had established that temperatures in the cooling systems had increased, adding that the incident was being investigated.
Belgium’s Le Soir newspaper reported that dozens of stores and supermarkets were affected, including five Spar outlets, multiple Shop & Go convenience stores attached to Q8 service stations, and a number of smaller Proxy Delhaize minimarkets.
“We started mobilising technicians at 1am,” Stephan Moelans, the chief executive of Sabcobel, which specialises in refrigeration system installations, told the paper. “We spent all night and morning disconnecting the affected installations from the grid.”
French ⁠police said in October that hackers had seized control of cooling units at ⁠up to 700 supermarkets in a large-scale attack that led to heavy losses of chilled and frozen foods and underlined the vulnerability of internet-connected systems.
Hackers had remotely overridden the settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets, pushing them from as low as -27C to well over 50C. The Intermarché, Coopérative U, Carrefour, Leclerc and Monoprix chains were among those affected.
Stores had to discard vast quantities of fresh meat, dairy and frozen products, with many suffering losses ranging from tens of thousands of euros to more than €130,000 (£109,000). Two stores in Alsace reported a combined loss of €270,000.
Most supermarket cold aisles are connected to the internet to allow remote maintenance and alerts for system failures. In the French attack, the hackers pirated controllers mostly supplied by the Danish company Danfoss.
after newsletter promotion
They disabled alarm systems before adjusting the thermostats or extending the defrost programme by hours. Danfoss said it had identified security flaws last year and had “long recommended” customers install updates.
The Paris prosecutor’s office has opened a formal investigatiion into the French attack, saying damage included “food losses and fires”, and the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, instructed France’s national cybersecurity agency, ANSSI, to investigate.
ANSSI subsequently confirmed that supermarkets using controllers from two other companies were also targeted in the attack.

articles.title_orig: Uganda says it has started withdrawing troops from Somalia
articles.title_zh: Uganda says it has started withdrawing troops from Somalia
articles.content_orig:
Uganda first deployed its troops to Somalia in 2007
Uganda has begun withdrawing its troops from Somalia after nearly two decades of military involvement in the country.
Uganda's acting army spokesperson Chris Magezi on Monday said the first group of troops deployed to Somalia through a bilateral arrangement had already arrived back home and others would follow in a few days' time.
He said all forces, including those under the African Union (AU) mission, would exit by the end of 2027 in the phased withdrawal.
Uganda was the first African country to deploy troops to Somalia under the African Union Mission in Somalia (Amisom), established in 2007 to help protect the country's transitional government from attacks by Islamist militants.
A first contingent of 109 Uganda People's Defence Forces (UPDF) troops reportedly left the capital, Mogadishu, on Friday, following an announcement by Uganda's army chief, Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba.
Last week, Kainerugaba said Uganda had begun pulling out its troops and would hand over security responsibilities to Somali forces.
"As we promised, we have started withdrawing UPDF from Somalia. After 20 years of a lot of blood and sacrifice, we are handing over security to our Somali brothers," he wrote on X.
On Monday, Magezi said this would mark the end of Uganda's operations in the Horn of Africa country, with Somalia expected to "assume full responsibility for security".
The withdrawal comes after Somalia President Sheikh Mohamud met his Ugandan counterpart Yoweri Museveni in Kampala last week.
The meeting was planned to discuss Somalia's security situation, as well as trade and economic ties between the two countries.
The Somali president reportedly sought to persuade Uganda to extend its military presence.
In remarks during the visit, Museveni urged Somali leaders and citizens to unite in the fight against the militant insurgency led by al-Shabab, which is part of al-Qaeda.
An estimated 4,500 troops are in Somalia under the Africa Union mission, alongside  about 2,000 deployed through bilateral arrangements.
Somalia has been battling a prolonged and deadly insurgency for more than two decades.
After Ugandan forces were first deployed to the country in 2007, they played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns.
They fought alongside the Somali National Army to recapture strategic territory and secure key government installations.
Ugandan troops were involved in successive Africa Union missions, including the African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (Atmis), which began with the aim of gradually transferring security responsibilities to Somalia.
This was replaced in 2025 by the African Union Support and Stabilisation Mission in Somalia (Aussom), which is focused on strengthening Somalia's security institutions and preparing its forces to take full responsibility for the country's security.
Aussom now faces uncertainty over its future funding, amid plans to wind down US and UN support.
A 12-month transition plan is due to begin in January, giving Somalia and the AU time to seek alternative sources of funding.

articles.title_orig: The Pokémon Company Is Counting Down To A Mysterious Date On Social Media
articles.title_zh: The Pokémon Company Is Counting Down To A Mysterious Date On Social Media
articles.content_orig:
The Pokémon Company is no stranger to a little over-hyping every now and then, but its latest bit of marketing has us seriously thinking that there is a big announcement in the pipeline.
You see, TPC is counting down to... something. As brought to our attention by Serebii 's Joe Merrick , the company has been sharing images on social media of its 30th anniversary icons , with a number underneath. Interestingly, these numbers decrease by the number of hours that have passed between each post — 1,025 on 18th October, 843 on 26th, 676 today.
Keeping the countdown going, this means that we'll hit zero on 30th November at 2pm UTC (thanks for doing the maths there, Joe!). The latest post even came with a full message under the logo, roughly translating to "Continue with Pokémon".
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 854k
Hmm . The big question is, what's this all about? 2pm UTC sure feels like the right time for a big announcement (it's when most eyes, worldwide, will be on it), and we can't imagine that TPC would put this much planning into something inconsequential.
What is it, then? Pokémon Ruby and Sapphire were rumoured to be coming to NSO last month, could it be that? Is it time we got another look at Winds and Waves , perhaps with a fire release date attached? Is there another full Pokémon Presents around the corner? Only time will tell, but it sure is an exciting prospect.
We'll be keeping an eye on the countdown throughout November and will let you know when any major news comes out of it.

articles.title_orig: Government making up China policy as it goes along, say MPs
articles.title_zh: Government making up China policy as it goes along, say MPs
articles.content_orig:
By SAM MERRIMAN, POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT
Published: 20:12 EDT, 1 November 2026 | Updated: 22:07 EDT, 1 November 2026
Ministers have been accused of jeopardising national security by prioritising 'diplomatic politeness' with China .
A report from MPs today criticises Labour's approach to Beijing as the 'worst of both worlds'.
In a devastating indictment of its dealings with the communist state, the chairman of the business, innovation, science and trade committee (Bist) said the 'Government keeps making up its China policy as it goes along'.
Firms have missed out on lucrative commercial deals as Britain has been left increasingly exposed to 'unquantified, unmanaged risk', the report adds.
Last night the committee put pressure on the Prime Minister to clarify his stance on closer dealings with the Chinese Communist Party.
'We await confirmation of how much continuity there is between the approaches to China of the Starmer and Burnham governments,' the MPs said.
Last year Labour, under Sir Keir Starmer, refused to publish a Government review of relations with China, releasing only a short summary and arguing that publishing the full findings could damage British interests.
In June, two men were convicted of running 'shadow policing' operations on British soil, spying on Chinese dissidents and MPs who supported them.
Labour ministers have been accused of jeopardising national security by prioritising 'diplomatic politeness' with China. Pictured: PM Andy Burnham, then Mayor of Manchester, with China's Consul General Tang Rui on April 17, 2026
Labour's Ed Miliband shakes hands with Wang Hongzhi, head of China's National Energy Administration, at the China-UK Energy Dialogue in Beijing, China on March 17, 2025
Labour was accused of pandering to China after plans for a new mega embassy on the old Royal Mint site were approved in January, despite spying fears. Pictured: A concept grapohic for the proposed embassy
Labour was accused of pandering to China after plans for a new mega embassy on the old Royal Mint site near the Tower of London were approved in January, despite spying fears.
Shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat has described the report as 'damning' and accused Labour of overseeing a dereliction of its duty to the public.
He told the Daily Mail: 'Labour are distracted and allowing Beijing to dictate terms, risking economic dependence on a hostile China. This is unacceptable. The Government's disjointed, last-minute approach leaves Britain weak and susceptible to Chinese control.'
The report warns that 'low-cost, increasingly sophisticated Chinese-connected technology has proliferated in the UK' and says the Government should create a register of high-risk firms to combat the threat associated with this.
It concludes: 'We are disappointed that, in failing to create a register of high-risk jurisdictions, the Government has prioritised diplomatic politeness over the UK's national security.' However, the Government last night rejected the Bist committee report and said it 'disagrees with its conclusion'.
The committee found that Labour has re-engaged with Beijing 'without establishing the rules of the game'.
Its chairman, Labour MP Liam Byrne, said: 'Businesses cannot plan for the future when the Government keeps making up its China policy as it goes along. Ministers promised clarity and consistency.
'Instead, we have opportunities missed, risks unmanaged and decisions left until the eleventh hour. Britain must shape its own relationship with China, or risk having that relationship shaped for us in Washington or Beijing.'
China's President Xi Jinping, right, and Britain's then Prime Minister Keir Starmer, left, shake hands before their meeting at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing on January 29, 2026
Bill Yuen, 65, (l) and Peter Wai, 41, (r) were convicted in June following a trial at the Old Bailey. Wai was found guilty of running a Chinese 'state intelligence service' on British soil while working as a UK Border Force officer, on the orders of former Hong Kong superintendent Yuen
The report also found products made with slave labour by repressed Uyghur Muslims ending up on British shelves. Pictured: Buildings north of Kashgar in China's northwestern Xinjiang region believed to be a re-education camp where mostly Muslim ethnic minorities are detained
Should Britain risk national security for economic ties and diplomatic relations with China?
Mr Byrne added that 'we should welcome trade that builds Britain's strength' but cease dealings that 'put that strength at risk'.
The committee recognised that disengaging from China is neither realistic nor desirable as annual trade with Beijing is now £140billion a year – about 7 per cent of total UK trade.
However it added that changes need to be made as the Government's decision-making on China – such as the takeover of British Steel from the firm's Chinese owners at a cost of £1.3million a day – has been characterised by 'reactivity, inconsistency, and opacity'.
MPs also raised concerns about the increasing adoption of cheap Chinese electric cars. These devices pose a risk to national security through spying and the ability to control vehicles remotely is a 'potential risk to life', the report adds.
The report is also damning on the risk of products made with slave labour by repressed Uyghur Muslims in the Xinjiang region ending up on British shelves.
In order to reset Britain's relationship with China, MPs have called on the Government to 'insist on fair trade' to create a 'level playing field'. Ministers should also 'prevent the transfer of sensitive technologies and data to China'.
A Government spokesman said: 'Our approach to China is consistent – we will co-operate where we can and challenge where we must.
'Our Trade Strategy makes clear that we will capitalise on every opportunity to grow our economy while never compromising on national security. Increased discussions with China allow us to directly raise concerns where they arise.'
