articles.title_zh: Iranians have left Doha talks, draft proposal for US deal being circulated, official says
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump said Washington had not “finished off” Iran because Tehran wanted to keep talking, while suggesting the United States might eventually take further action.
In an interview with Miranda Devine on the Pod Force One podcast, released Monday, Trump said: “We’ve been nice because we haven’t finished them off because, you know, they wanted to talk and they keep talking, talking, talking. At some point, we’ll have to do that.”
He added that Iran wanted to make a deal, but said, “We’ll see about a deal.”
Trump also said the United States could not allow Iran to have nuclear weapons.
Russia’s foreign ministry said on Monday that reports of new military action against Iran were a cause for extreme concern.
Moscow called for greater diplomatic efforts to normalize the situation in the region.
The United Arab Emirates will be better prepared than before for whatever follows in the US-Israeli war with Iran, Energy Minister Suhail al-Mazrouei said on Monday.
Speaking at the Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition and Conference, he said the course of the war was unpredictable.
At certain points, he added, the UAE’s exports had performed better than before the war.
Iran’s position on defending its national security, sovereignty and territorial integrity has not changed, and Tehran will make no compromises on those issues, the deputy secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council said on Monday after meeting China’s foreign minister in Beijing.
Ali Bagheri Kani also described the killing of former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei by the United States and Israel as a “war crime.”
The spokesman for Iran parliament’s national security committee warned on Monday that a renewed war could spread geographically and strike areas not previously considered targets.
Hassan Ghashghavi said there were places “perhaps no one has thought about so far,” but said he would not discuss details.
He said Iran’s offensive and defensive capabilities had improved since the 12-day war and that a new conflict would bring “more surprises.”
Ghashghavi said an order by Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei for an immediate and effective response to threats, without geographical limits, had been issued for implementation and should not remain at the level of analysis and commentary.
The gold, jewelry, silver and coin dealers’ union in Iran’s northeastern city of Mashhad has banned the sale and display of gold products featuring designs associated with the Pahlavi era or the Lion and Sun, according to an official notice to businesses in the sector.
The union said businesses found displaying or selling the items would face action.
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said on Monday that parties to the Middle East conflict should pursue political solutions rather than resume fighting, during a meeting in Beijing with Iranian national security official Ali Bagheri Kani, China’s Xinhua news agency reported.
Wang also said China supports Iran in safeguarding its sovereignty and security.
Iranian negotiators left Doha on Sunday, but not because of difficulties in talks aimed at ending the US-Israeli war on Iran, Reuters reported on Monday, citing an official briefed on the discussions.
A draft proposal was being circulated for feedback, and a follow-up meeting was possible, the official added.
Iran should extend its missile range beyond 2,000 kilometers and reconsider its nuclear doctrine, including developing the capability to build nuclear weapons, a lawmaker said on Monday.
Mohammad Motamedizadeh said Israel was “at the tip of our blade” and that Iran should also target “the heart of America.” He said Iran could target adversaries’ interests in the United States and Europe if threatened.
He added that there was no reason for Iran to remain in the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty.
He also described Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei’s remarks about responding to threats “at any level” as a sign of a shift in Iran’s nuclear posture.

articles.title_orig: Initial results show Bulgaria's president Yotova wins runoff election
articles.title_zh: Initial results show Bulgaria's president Yotova wins runoff election
articles.content_orig:
Acting President Iliana Yotova is the apparent winner of Bulgaria ’s presidential runoff, initial results of the vote count on Sunday showed.
The race for the largely ceremonial post had pitted Yotova, an ally of Prime Minister Rumen Radev, against Andrey Gyurov, a banker and former caretaker prime minister backed by the pro-Western opposition.
Yotova gained between 57.4% and 58.2% of the vote, according to estimates from several polling institutes, well ahead of Gyurov, who garnered between 38.6% and 39.6%.
If confirmed by official results, Yotova would become Bulgaria’s first elected female head of state.
Gyurov conceded defeat saying that “this is how the Bulgarian citizens have voted,” and added that the results had to be accepted as they stood.
The war in Ukraine, close to Bulgaria’s borders, played a significant role in the election in this country on NATO’s eastern flank.
Throughout the campaign, Yotova repeatedly advocated a peaceful solution for Ukraine through negotiations with Russia. She said she wanted to be a “President of Peace” for Bulgaria.
Gyurov, in contrast, signalled closer alignment with Western partners and stronger support for Ukraine in the face of Russia’s war of aggression.
The vote was the first major test for the Moscow-friendly Progressive Bulgaria party of Prime Minister Rumen Radev, which endorsed Yotova. The 62-year-old took over the presidency in January, when Radev stepped down to run for parliament.
Observers expect her to continue Radev’s policy of keeping Bulgaria on its European path, while also supporting better relations with Russia and the lifting of sanctions.
The election in this south-eastern EU country was overshadowed by the conflict in Ukraine. In recent weeks, drone attacks on merchant ships have become increasingly frequent in Bulgaria’s economic zone in the Black Sea, as well as in that of neighbouring Romania.
Bulgaria’s presidency is primarily ceremonial. The head of state has no executive powers, and all major policies must be approved by parliament. However, direct election gives the president greater political authority. The president leads the armed forces, can veto legislation, signs international treaties and appoints ambassadors.
Presidents in Bulgaria are directly elected for a five-year term and can serve no more than two terms.

articles.title_orig: Robots strut their stuff, race up sacred China mountain, some carrying eggs and watermelons
articles.title_zh: Robots strut their stuff, race up sacred China mountain, some carrying eggs and watermelons
articles.content_orig:
Dozens of robots took on more than 3,000 steps up one of China's most famous peaks Monday, many carrying eggs and watermelons in a race organizers billed as a test of real-world machine endurance, state media showed.
For hundreds of years, Mount Tai -- the tallest peak in China's eastern Shandong province -- was an important pilgrimage for Chinese emperors, and it features prominently in Chinese mythology.
But the rugged terrain would prove a stern test for some competitors. One humanoid robot wearing a bandana collapsed in a heap on the cobbled route before engineers rushed in to repair it, while another tumbled down a flight of stairs and came to rest beside a rubbish bin.
The UNESCO World Heritage site hosted technologies of the future as part of a new World Mountain Robot Challenge, footage from state broadcaster CCTV showed.
Over a 2.4-mile course with more than 1,970 feet of ascent, robots and their engineers from around 90 teams were tasked with either completing the route as fast as possible or transporting fragile goods such as fresh eggs and watermelons to the summit.
A canine robot made by Beijing Lingyi Technology -- a subsidiary of industry giant Unitree -- completed the course in 43 minutes, 41 seconds, to win the four-legged speed category.
Most tourists take at least two hours to complete the route, according to CCTV.
The fastest humanoid robot -- belonging to Beijing-based team Zhishen Lingyue -- completed a shorter race course in 27 minutes and 26 seconds.
Organizers called Mount Tai's rocky terrain a "natural extreme testing ground" that could help train robots for real-world use, local media reported.
The race, organized by the state-run China Media Group, featured cash prizes for winners in several categories, including the fastest robots and the best load-carrying four-legged machine.

articles.title_orig: Iranian Tankers Bypass U.S. Naval Blockade to Transport Gas to China
articles.title_zh: Iranian Tankers Bypass U.S. Naval Blockade to Transport Gas to China
articles.content_orig:
A report by Fox News, citing the advocacy group “United Against Nuclear Iran” (UANI), reveals that at least nine tankers carrying Iranian oil or liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) have successfully bypassed U.S. maritime restrictions since the reimposition of the American naval blockade in July 2026.
According to the report, published on the evening of Sunday, November 1, 2026, tankers belonging to the Islamic Republic’s so-called “ghost fleet” are utilising maritime routes around Malaysia to transport sanctioned Iranian energy cargoes to China.
Following months of investigation, UANI published images of a tanker named “SOGL,” which departed from the port of Asaluyeh in late August 2026, carrying approximately 500,000 barrels of liquefied petroleum gas. After breaking through the U.S. naval blockade, the vessel reached Malaysian waters.
Jemima Shelley, a senior analyst at UANI, told Fox News that the tanker refuelled in waters near Malaysia and, after receiving support services, delivered its cargo to the port of Qinzhou in China.
According to Shelley, some smaller Iranian tankers turn off their tracking systems, sail under false flags, or conduct ship-to-ship transfers at sea to evade detection.
The UANI analyst noted that while the U.S. blockade has severely curtailed Iran’s crude oil exports, certain smaller tankers still manage to slip through.
Fox News further reported that China now serves as the destination for almost “all of Iran’s oil and LPG exports,” with Malaysian maritime corridors playing a critical role in sustaining this trade.

articles.content_orig:
Sales momentum among leading carmakers contrasts with a domestic market downturn that is accelerating industry consolidation, analysts say
Shenzhen-based electric vehicle (EV) giant BYD handed over 490,168 cars to customers at home and abroad last month, up 11 per cent year on year, while Hangzhou-headquartered Geely delivered 310,183 petrol and electric cars worldwide in the same period, up 1 per cent from a year earlier, according to company statements.
“Top players, banking on their new models and advantages in cost and technology, showed their resilience in sales,” said Gao Shen, an independent analyst in Shanghai. “Their sales rises have ratcheted up pressure on weak carmakers that are struggling to survive [in a fiercely competitive] domestic market.”

articles.title_orig: China touts AI milestone: models generate more tokens than used in training
articles.title_zh: China touts AI milestone: models generate more tokens than used in training
articles.content_orig:
Average daily token calls exceed 175 trillion, government-backed report says, indicating growing demand for AI services
For the first time, the amount of inference data generated by artificial intelligence systems in China has surpassed the amount of data used to train those systems, according to a new government-backed report, illustrating how the country is increasingly adopting AI at scale.
The report released on Saturday by the China Centre for Information Industry Development (CCID), which operates under China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT), cited recent official data showing that China’s average daily token calls exceeded 175 trillion, an increase of more than 1,000 times from early 2024.
Inference refers to the process of running trained AI models to respond to user requests, which involves processing units of data known as tokens. As AI adoption accelerates, the volume of token calls, which refers to AI usage through public cloud service providers, provides an indication of growing demand for AI services.
_src_links: China touts AI milestone: models generate more tokens than used in training

articles.title_orig: Russia and Ukraine say emergency alert apps were hit by apparent cyber-attacks
articles.title_zh: Russia and Ukraine say emergency alert apps were hit by apparent cyber-attacks
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine and Russia say their emergency warning apps have been hit by cyber-attacks, causing false alerts to be issued
Moscow says a "massive cyber-attack" has affected its app but insists its wider alert system is "operating as normal" . A Ukrainian espionage group claims the messages included fake warnings of nuclear strikes inside Russia
This comes shortly after Ukraine's air raid warning app sent out false warnings of a radiation threat in Kyiv , following an apparent hack
Ukraine has blamed Russia for the hack on its app, while Moscow is yet to say who it believes is behind the cyber-attack on its system
The alerts in Ukraine were sent out just minutes before the end of a localised ceasefire in the front-line Kherson region, our Ukraine reporter Abdujalil Abdurasulov writes
Edited by Toby Mann and Yvette Tan
While we wait for further information on the apparent cyber attacks in Russia and Ukraine, here's the latest on the strikes that were reported overnight.
In a statement on Telegram, Russia's Ministry of Defence says it struck a Ukrainian military cargo vessel at sea 58km south of Odesa overnight.
It says the vessel was "delivering cargo intended for the Ukrainian Armed Forces".
Another strike hit a storage site for Ukrainian missile launch systems in the Odesa village of Tuzly, it says.
Meanwhile, a Telegram channel for the city of Odesa says four people were injured in strikes in Odesa overnight. "All received prompt medical assistance," the update says.
It adds that two private homes, a garage and city infrastructure also sustained "significant damage".
The false alerts started at approximately 22:47 (20:47 GMT) on Sunday, with red-level air raids apparently issued nationwide, in Ukrainian.
Additional warnings were issued in Kyiv, with the first reading: "Radiation threat. Radiation threat declared in Kyiv."
The next message, written in Russian, came at 22:48 , which read: "Hi! There will be a nuclear alert across Ukraine. Don't worry, it's Oreshnik flying". Oreshnik is the name of a Russian intermediate-range ballistic missile capable of carrying nuclear or conventional warheads.
A third alert, at 22:49 , again in Ukrainian, said "Chemical threat. There is a threat of a chemical attack on Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 22:49 , a fourth alert stated there was a "street fighting threat. Street fighting is taking place in Kyiv. Don't go outside."
At 23:53 a series of all clear messages were then delivered to users' phones, which were connected to each of the previous Kyiv alerts, individually declaring each threat clear.
We don't know much about the alerts sent out in Russia. But as we reported earlier, a Ukrainian espionage group claimed fake warnings of nuclear strikes inside Russia had been sent to users.
Dan Johnson Ukraine correspondent, reporting from Kyiv
Ukraineâs air raid alert app usually warns of incoming Russian drones or missiles.
Last night it issued alerts of a radiological threat, a chemical attack and street fighting here in Kyiv.
The warnings were followed by all clear messages just over an hour later.
The air force issued a statement saying the app had been hacked and reassured citizens there was no imminent threat of nuclear war, blaming Russian interference.
Hours later, Russiaâs emergencies ministry claimed it had also suffered a cyber attack and said people were receiving emails containing fake information.
Itâs not clear if the two incidents are connected.
Oleksander Merezhko, chair of the Ukrainian parliament's foreign affairs committee, has told the BBC the attack did not cause panic or extreme reactions.
Merezhko says Ukrainians, especially in Kyiv, are used to "practically non-stop alerts".
"Secondly, this message was in Russian language which immediately aroused suspicions," he says.
"It's a very unpleasant fact but it is part of cyber war and people in Ukraine understand that. It is possible and we are quite prepared for such possibilities," adds Merezhko, a member of President Volodymyr Zelensky's Servant of the People party,
Russia and Ukraine both say their emergency alert systems have been hit by cyber-attacks. Here's what we know so far:
The BBC's Newsday programme has just spoken to Herbert Lin, a senior research scholar for cyber policy and security at Stanford University, who describes the hacking of Ukraine's air strike alert system as "concerning".

âWe donât know how they did it yetâ¦ Maybe in the future theyâll be able to do it more but we just donât know yet.â

Russia said drone strikes hit an "industrial enterprise" east of Moscow overnight, which Ukrainian media identified as the Kstovo oil refinery.
The governor of Russia's Nizhny Novgorod region - home to the Kstovo plant - described a "massive" drone attack during the night and morning.

Some connections were restored on Sunday.

Emergency alert apps in Ukraine and Russia have been hacked, according to reports.
The Ukraine government's Center for Strategic Communications has blamed Russia for the hack in a post on its X account, saying one of the alerts was a "message in Russian about Oreshnik".
A few hours later, Moscow also said that its emergency alert app had been hit by a "massive cyber-attack" - but did not immediately say who might be behind it.
Ukraine's Centre for Strategic Communications has blamed Russia for the hack in a post on its X account.
It posted a picture showing some of the alerts that had showed up on Ukraine's air raid warning app and asked residents to "disregard" any "strange messages" they might see in the app.

"The hacking of the mobile app has not had, and cannot have, any impact on the operation of the public alert system," it said on its Telegram channel.
It said specialists were working to restore normal operation of the mobile app but the situation was "under control".

(Kitco NewsWire) - Spot gold and silver prices were sharply lower in late U.S. trading Friday, as a technology-led equity market selloff intensified liquidation pressure across precious metals, offsetting the support normally provided by falling Treasury yields and heightened geopolitical uncertainty. Crude oil prices climbed more than 2% following another tanker attack in the Strait of Hormuz, adding to inflation concerns and expectations that Federal Reserve monetary policy will remain restrictive. Spot gold was trading near $3,879.90 an ounce, down $141.60, or 3.52%, while spot silver was trading near $49.015, down $3.150, or 6.06%, on the session.
Friday's U.S. economic reports presented a mixed picture of moderating wage growth and weakening regional manufacturing activity. The employment cost index increased 0.8% in the third quarter, matching expectations and slowing from 0.9% in the second quarter. The October Chicago purchasing managers' index declined to 55.3 from 58.8 in September, missing expectations near 56.1 but remaining above the 50-point threshold separating expansion from contraction. Friday's softer wage and manufacturing readings followed Thursday's stronger-than-expected third-quarter gross domestic product report, which showed the U.S. economy expanding at a 3.4% annualized pace , compared with 2.2% in the second quarter. September headline personal consumption expenditures inflation accelerated to 3.6% annually, while core PCE inflation increased to 3.1%, reinforcing concerns about persistent underlying price pressure.
Market positioning remains divided between resilient economic growth, persistent inflation and the growing risk of financial-market instability. The Federal Reserve left its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.75% to 4.00% Wednesday , with two policymakers favoring an immediate 25-basis-point increase. Interest rate futures continued to reflect substantial expectations for further tightening in December, although Friday's moderating employment costs and sharp equity-market decline provided counterweights to the inflationary implications of strong GDP growth and higher energy prices. Treasury yields fell as investors sought the relative safety of government bonds, with the benchmark 10-year yield retreating toward 4.93% and the two-year yield approaching 4.58%. However, gold continued to decline, suggesting that forced liquidation, portfolio rebalancing and the broader outlook for restrictive monetary policy outweighed immediate safe-haven demand.
The Strait of Hormuz and U.S.-Iran situation remained a major source of energy-market uncertainty Friday after another commercial tanker was attacked in the strategic waterway. The vessel was struck by explosive devices attached to its hull by a small boat, highlighting the continuing vulnerability of commercial shipping despite regional diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions. Responsibility for the attack had not been established. The incident intensified concerns that renewed military confrontation involving Iran and the United States could further disrupt Middle Eastern energy exports, particularly as markets assessed the possibility of additional military action following the Nov. 3 U.S. midterm elections. Negotiations involving Washington, Tehran and regional mediators have yet to produce a confirmed settlement, leaving disagreements over sanctions, maritime security and the future of commercial access through Hormuz unresolved.
Crude oil futures rose more than 2% Friday, reaching their highest settlements since late April as traders assessed the possibility of renewed disruptions to Gulf energy supplies. December Brent crude futures gained $2.76, or 2.4%, to settle at $117.64 a barrel after reaching $118.00 intraday. The more actively traded January Brent contract advanced $2.63 to $113.43, while Nymex WTI futures increased $2.12, or 2.08%, to settle at $104.12. Brent gained approximately 13.6% during October, while WTI rose 15.2%, reflecting persistent concerns about Middle Eastern supply security and the inflationary consequences of the regional conflict.
For gold, the latest Hormuz attack reinforced underlying geopolitical demand, but higher crude prices also heightened the risk that inflation will remain persistent and the Federal Reserve will maintain restrictive monetary policy. The sharp decline in bullion despite falling Treasury yields indicates that broader financial-market liquidation was the more immediate influence on Friday's trading. Silver suffered considerably greater losses as weakness in precious metals coincided with concerns about industrial demand, equity-market valuations and restrictive financing conditions. The widening gold-silver ratio reflected silver's greater sensitivity to deteriorating risk sentiment and concerns about manufacturing activity.
North American equity markets finished sharply lower Friday as disappointing corporate earnings and concerns about artificial intelligence-related investment triggered heavy selling in technology shares. The Dow Jones Industrial Average declined approximately 1.1% to close at 51,770.31, while the S&P 500 fell 1.8% to 7,580.07, its largest daily decline since June. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 2.9% to finish near 25,437, as weakness in semiconductor and major technology shares dominated trading. Intel plunged nearly 29% following disappointing profit guidance, while concerns surrounding Amazon's capital spending added to pressure on the technology sector. The Russell 2000 declined 1.7% to 2,811.84, indicating that selling extended beyond large-cap growth companies. Canada's S&P/TSX Composite Index also fell sharply, losing more than 2% as weakness in precious metals mining and other resource shares compounded the broader deterioration in risk sentiment.
European equity markets closed mostly lower Friday as technology-sector weakness and concerns about elevated energy prices weighed on investor sentiment. The pan-European Stoxx 600 declined approximately 0.4% to 646.73, while Germany's DAX lost 0.9% to finish near 25,819. France's CAC 40 slipped 0.1% to approximately 7,962, while the U.K.'s FTSE 100 outperformed, advancing 0.1% to around 10,736. The Euro Stoxx 50 fell approximately 1.2%, reflecting heavier losses among major continental companies. European technology shares were particularly weak as the U.S. semiconductor selloff affected global valuations, while higher crude prices added to concerns about inflation, corporate margins and the outlook for regional monetary policy. Despite Friday's losses, the Stoxx 600 finished October higher, reflecting gains earlier in the month.
The key outside markets see Nymex WTI crude oil futures higher and settling at $104.12 a barrel, while December Brent crude futures finished at $117.64. The yield on the benchmark 10-year U.S. Treasury note declined toward the 4.93% area as demand for government bonds increased during the equity selloff. The U.S. dollar was comparatively firm, supported by defensive demand and expectations for restrictive Federal Reserve policy. Bears' next near-term downside price objective is to maintain prices below $3,890.00, with deeper downside targets at $3,800.00 and then $3,780.00. articles.title_orig: ‘We Spy Better’: Trump Taunts China, Russia as Netanyahu Pushes for Iran Strikes
articles.title_zh: ‘We Spy Better’: Trump Taunts China, Russia as Netanyahu Pushes for Iran Strikes
articles.content_orig:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said President Donald Trump would like to resolve the Iranian war "diplomatically," and prefers not to use military force.
Speaking over the weekend, Rubio told reporters that "He [Trump] hasn't made a decision...what the president expresses to you is incredible confidence that if we needed to do something militarily, we would have the ability to do it, and we really we have everything we need to be successful. But we would prefer to do it peacefully."
The remarks come as reports suggest both sides are gearing up for additional military strikes after the midterm elections.
On Saturday, Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei called for Tehran's armed forces to meet "any level or type of threat" with "an immediate, impactful, and geographically unrestricted response."
He also ordered that its military database be updated so that "all kinds of physical and non-physical assets of the U.S.-Zionist enemy are brought within the reach of the Armed Forces," referring to U.S. and Israeli forces.
Washington has not explicitly stated it plans to resume attacks on Iran, but reports from The Wall Street Journal and The New York Times indicate the U.S. is preparing for possible renewed military actions after the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
On Sunday, Trump told the Right Side Broadcasting Network. "We've had such a victory, and we'll put it away very soon, one way or the other."
"Either they'll make a deal, or we'll just end it," he added.
On Sunday, Iran's foreign ministry designated the U.K.'s Military Intelligence Services as a "hostile group" and accused the Royal Navy and Air Force of supporting "terrorist organizations." In a Telegram post , the ministry said that the move was a response to what it called London's "malicious" actions, including the designation of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps as a "terrorist organization."
Tehran has separately accused the U.K. of participating in the U.S.-Iran war by allowing American forces access to British military and logistical bases.
The U.K. had allowed U.S. forces to use RAF Fairford and Diego Garcia for what were described as "defensive" strikes on Iran, according to the BBC.

articles.title_orig: King to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology
articles.title_zh: King to address slavery in Antigua as PM says he is open to possible UK apology
articles.content_orig:
King Charles III is to speak with "unflinching honesty" and "sincere sorrow" on the lasting pain of the transatlantic slave trade during the final leg of his Caribbean tour in Antigua, Buckingham Palace has said.
The King will address Commonwealth leaders on Tuesday in a speech that will touch on the issue.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham earlier wrote in the Guardian that he was "open" to the possibility of the UK formally apologising for its role in slavery - a change in the government's stance.
It is understood the Palace was told in advance of Burnham's comments in an opinion piece on Friday night, and that the King has not made any changes to his speech in light of them.
The British government has never formally apologised for slavery or offered to pay reparations.
Burnham has previously stuck with the policy of his predecessors and stopped short of offering any consideration of reparation payments.
In an address to the nation to mark Antigua and Barbuda's independence day, Prime Minister Gaston Browne said the history of slavery was painful and "its consequences have not disappeared with the passage of time".
He said the country's pursuit of reparatory justice deserved "seriousness, sensitivity and sustained international engagement".
Browne went on to say that his government was having these conversations in bilateral discussions with the UK and other Commonwealth countries at the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch described "endless talk about apologies" as a "distraction" from solving current problems.
She told BBC Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg: "The transatlantic slave trade happened centuries ago. It is time for the Commonwealth to start looking forwards, not endlessly backwards."
The King will make his speech at the CHOGM.
He "will not shy away from confronting the most shameful aspects of the past during this visit", a Palace spokesperson said.
"You may therefore expect him to address them in his speech with unflinching honesty, sincere sorrow and respect for the wider discussions that will be taking place between relevant governments on this issue at CHOGM and beyond."
When asked about the King's reaction to the prime minister's comments, the spokesperson said it would "not be appropriate" for the King to address matters of policy relating to the government's position.
The Caribbean tour has again thrust the King into the difficult debates over the UK's colonial legacy in the region.
On his first stop in the Bahamas, the King delivered a speech in which he spoke of the "suffering of the past".
In Guyana, he visited the site of a Slave Rebellion , where hundreds of enslaved people were killed.
Buckingham Palace said it was a moment for the King to learn more about the history of slavery and resistance. His engagements have also covered the environment, opportunities for young people and trade relationships with the UK.
Royal sources have stressed that the decisions around making an apology were a matter for government, not the Palace.
"His Majesty is well practised on the diplomatic tightrope," a Royal aide said. "He is up for challenging visits with complex issues and relationships in play. He sees it as his role to bat for Britain, the Realms and wider Commonwealth."
In a piece for the Guardian published on Friday night, Burnham described the transatlantic slave trade as a "brutal and barbaric violation", and said Britain "must face up to the past".
His separate pledge in his article to strengthen the work of the Commonwealth as an organisation will be welcomed by the King, who views the collection of 56 countries as a powerful vehicle for change.
The King will be giving the opening speech at CHOGM, which gathers leaders from those 56 states every two years in a different part of the Commonwealth.
The biennial meeting's official theme this year is Accelerating Partnerships and Investment for a Prosperous Commonwealth.
Queen Camilla is with the King in Antigua and, as the couple attended a church service on Sunday morning ahead of joining celebrations to mark Independence Day on the island, there was a reminder of what the intended focus of the week will be.
Bishop of North Eastern Caribbean and Aruba, Ernest Flemming, told the congregation the "prosperity" of the Commonwealth must be a "shared prosperity".
"True partnership requires mutual respect, it requires listening, it requires fairness."
A Buckingham Palace spokesperson said: "Institutions are under strain across the globe. The Commonwealth has scale and breadth, but is also small enough for leaders to know each other and co-operate together."
The King, they said, "contributes ideas and encouragement on a wide range of issues, delivering practical results which help improve the lives of millions".
Later on Sunday, the King was left drenched and without an umbrella when a torrential downpour interrupted an Independence Day ceremony.
The Queen was swiftly given an umbrella when the rain started, while the King was seen gesturing to be given one of his own.
It has been a difficult few months for the King, with developments surrounding his brother, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor , and the publication of a book by his former brother-in-law, Earl Spencer.
In addition, his son, the Duke of Sussex, made a surprise move back to the UK with his wife Meghan and their two children in August.
Asked whether the King was confident that his approach to family matters had been the right one in terms of public attitudes towards the institution, the response was concise. "Yes," a senior aide told the BBC. "That is why he takes the actions he does - and has done."
On the serious allegations that have emerged about Meghan's father , Thomas Markle, the Palace did not want to get involved publicly: "We wouldn't comment on private family matters."
The King is also still being treated for cancer. He was diagnosed in early 2024 and the Palace says he remains on a "positive trajectory".
In hot and humid conditions, he will soon celebrate his 78th birthday and will have carried out about 36 engagements by the end of this nine-day tour of the Caribbean.

articles.content_orig:
Foreign diplomats are also gearing up for the November 18-19 summit taking place amid tightened security in the southern Chinese city
Construction workers have been working late into the night in downtown Shenzhen as the city makes its final preparations for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in two weeks’ time.
On a weekday night, a South China Morning Post reporter saw at least 50 construction workers gathered at an intersection about 1km (just over half a mile) from the Apec venues in the central district of Futian, laying down pebbles and planting trees along the pavements.
The main road that leads up to the newly built Shenzhen International Communication Centre has also been dug up, with a new layer of asphalt being laid on top. All the lamp posts were decorated with flags reading “Apec China”.

articles.title_orig: Poll: Are You Happy with Your PS Plus Essential Games for November 2026?
articles.title_zh: Poll: Are You Happy with Your PS Plus Essential Games for November 2026?
articles.content_orig:
November's PS Plus Essential games were revealed earlier this week, and I think it's quite an interesting selection.
That's because all three games offer something completely different. We've got a fairly big-name headliner, a collection of remastered adventures, and a highly-rated indie on our hands.
Dead Island 2 is up first. This punchy sequel combines hyper violent zombie-slaying with tongue-in-cheek storytelling across an apocalyptic Los Angeles.
It's a good laugh — especially if you team up with a couple of friends online — and a solid action romp.
Subscribe to Push Square on YouTube 172k
Tomb Raider 4-6 Remastered is next on the list, and while Lara Croft's fourth, fifth, and sixth outings are rarely mentioned with the same kind of reverence as her original trilogy, they're still packed with nostalgic platforming goodness.
And last but certainly not least — go and check the review scores — is Monster Train 2 . This is a deck-building roguelike full of fantastical creatures, and it's super addictive once you've wrapped your head around the turn-based mechanics.
I get it: some people hear "deck-building" and "roguelike", and they turn away — but there's a reason this hugely expanded sequel is so highly regarded.

articles.title_orig: Iran Update, November 1, 2026
articles.title_zh: Iran Update, November 1, 2026
articles.source: Institute for the Study of War
articles.content_orig:
The Institute for the Study of War (ISW) and The Critical Threats Project (CTP) at the American Enterprise Institute are publishing updates Monday through Friday to provide analysis on the war with Iran and the broader Middle East. Weekday updates cover events from the past 24-hour period, whereas weekend updates are abbreviated and cover the Houthi-Saudi conflict and major breaking developments related to the war with Iran.
See “Iranian Strike Campaign” and “Arabian Peninsula” sections.
Nothing significant to report.
Assessed Iranian War Aims:
Iran likely struck a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz on November 1 as part of its efforts to disrupt civilian shipping. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organization (UKMTO) reported on November 1 that an unidentified projectile struck a vessel in the Strait of Hormuz.[1] The Iranian regime calculates that it can pressure the United States into a diplomatic settlement that favors Iran by disrupting shipping and keeping oil prices high. Iran continues to be the only threat to civilian shipping in the strait.
Nothing significant to report.
Nothing significant to report.
Nothing significant to report.
Nothing significant to report.
The Houthis are continuing to attempt to advance southeastward from Taiz Governorate into Lahij Governorate, potentially to set conditions to besiege or capture Aden City. A Marib-based Yemeni journalist reported that Houthi fighters advanced onto elevated terrain in al Maqatirah District, Lahij Governorate, on November 1.[2] Pro-Yemeni government media reported that Yemeni government reinforcements deployed to the district later on November 1.[3] The source did not specify whether Yemeni government-aligned forces recaptured territory in al Maqatirah District, which suggests that the area remains contested at the time of this writing.[4] Yemeni government-aligned forces reportedly repelled another Houthi attempt to advance southeastward from southern Taiz Governorate into al Maqatirah District on October 30. The Houthis likely seek to capture terrain that overlooks Tur al Balah District and leads to Aden City. Such territory would support a potential Houthi effort to besiege or capture Aden City.[5]
Yemeni government-aligned forces continued to engage Houthi fighters in central Jawf Governorate on November 1. A Marib-based Yemeni journalist reported that Yemeni government-aligned forces repelled a Houthi attempt to advance to Jabal Huwayshiyan from the northeast. Jabal Huwayshiyan is a mountain range overlooking al Hazm, the governorate’s capital.[6] Yemeni government-aligned forces recaptured Jabal Huwayshiyan between October 30 and 31.[7] Yemeni government-aligned forces are likely attempting to recapture territory in central Jawf Governorate as part of an effort to set conditions to recapture al Hazm.[8]
Saudi Joint Forces Command spokesperson Major General Turki al Maliki announced that Saudi Arabia targeted unspecified “vital resources” in Houthi-controlled Dhamar and Hudaydah governorates on November 1.[9] Pro-Yemeni government media and Houthi media reported that Saudi Arabia struck Houthi troop concentrations in Dhamar Governorate.[10] Houthi media separately reported that Saudi Arabia struck oil infrastructure in Bajil District, Hudaydah Governorate.[11] Saudi Arabia previously struck Houthi oil and fuel storage infrastructure in Yemen on October 13, likely to both maximize economic pressure on the Houthi political organization and constrain the Houthis’ ability to sustain their military forces.[12]
Saudi air defenses intercepted one Houthi ballistic missile and one drone launched toward Saudi Arabia’s southern region on November 1. [13] The Houthis have not claimed the attack as of this writing. The Houthis have repeatedly targeted Saudi critical infrastructure as part of the Houthis’ ongoing strike campaign to compel Saudi Arabia to halt military operations against the Houthis and accept the Houthis’ demands, which include lifting Saudi controls on Houthi-controlled ports and airports and granting the Houthis control over Yemen’s oil and gas resources.[14]

articles.title_orig: Huawei in the Dock
articles.title_zh: Huawei in the Dock
articles.content_orig:
Good evening. If all had gone according to plan, the United States v Wanzhou Meng and Huawei Technologies would have opened in a federal courtroom in the waning months of President Donald Trump’s first term. And what a trial it would have been: an heir to one of China’s most successful and strategically important companies, detained in Canada and extradited to the U.S., on trial for allegedly lying to banks about Huawei operations in Iran that were in violation of American sanctions on the country. But Xi Jinping forestalled that humiliating spectacle by ordering the arrest of two Canadians in China, Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor, and not releasing them until the U.S. and Canada allowed Meng, the daughter of Huawei’s founder, to return to China in September 2021. Five years later the United States v Huawei Technologies , minus Meng, is finally underway. Noah Berman reports from the courtroom in Brooklyn.
In other articles, Leon Panetta speaks with Bob Davis about his dealings with China as a Congressman, White House Chief-of-Staff, CIA Director and Secretary of Defense.
Noah Berman on DayOne , the Singaporean data center operator that is helping Chinese companies realise their AI ambitions.
In The Big Picture , Savannah Billman writes about the enormous popularity of AI-generated “short dramas” in China.
Lizzi C. Lee and Simon Hedlin on the barriers to a common-sense Sino-U.S. AI safety agreement .
And finally, be sure to catch up on the latest episode of our weekly podcast , with Peiyue Wu talking about her recent cover on dual-use farms in China.
Want this emailed directly to your inbox? Sign up to receive our free newsletter.
In 2021 Meng Wanzhou, daughter of Huawei Technologies founder Ren Zhengfei, signed a “statement of facts” to resolve U.S. charges against her. According to that statement, “Ms. Meng [told HSBC] … Huawei’s relationship with Skycom was ‘normal business cooperation’ and … she described Skycom as a … ‘third party Huawei works with’ in Iran … Those statements were untrue because, as Ms. Meng knew, … Huawei controlled Skycom.” The U.S. let Meng go regardless because the Chinese government made it clear that it would not release two Canadian hostages until she was freed. Five years later the U.S. government’s case against Huawei is finally underway in New York, with Meng safely back in China.
Leon Panetta fought with, and engaged with China over a long career in politics. The former Congressman, White House Chief of Staff, CIA Director and Defense Secretary talks with Bob Davis about why China thinks President Trump is good for China.
“If China senses weakness, they’ll take advantage of it,” Panetta says. “Right now, China is in a stronger position because we’re locked in a war in Iran, our economy is being impacted by that war, and there’s a lot of unpredictability about the U.S. China has been able to take advantage in areas where once we had some influence, particularly in the Pacific.”
Illustration by Lauren Crow
The U.S. government doesn’t want America’s best chips to power Chinese data centers that would then help Chinese companies hone their AI models and applications. DayOne, a Singapore-based data center provider, profits from this by building data centers in Southeast Asia where Chinese AI firms can legally access America’s best chips. Noah Berman looks at DayOne and the IPO prospectus it has just issued. “DayOne’s rise,” he writes, “illustrates how companies can profit, and even gain backing from American investors, as U.S. export controls lead Chinese companies to seek access to data centers overseas.”
Are you, like the Old Dad who writes this newsletter, also a parent who dreads the short videos on YouTube and elsewhere that so easily reel in your kids? Alas, writes Savannah Billman , if China is anything to go by — as it increasingly is when it comes to tech trends — the madness is only going to get worse. Almost 900 million (!) Chinese people are watching AI-generated “short dramas”, issued as a seemingly endless stream of two-minute videos, on a new generation of apps tailored to the new genre. Over the first half of this year alone about 267,000 AI short videos were released. Ugh.
Recent steps taken towards the establishment of a U.S.-China AI incident-reporting channel are important, write Lizzi C. Lee and Simon Hedlin . But, they add, there is “a more pressing issue: frontier AI companies currently do not provide the information they need”.

Like other middle powers, the Central Asian nation is striving to build a new AI economy while bridging a widening US-China tech divide
Driving along the wide boulevards of Astana during a recent trip to the Kazakh capital, signs of China’s growing commercial footprint were everywhere.
Chinese cars were becoming a common sight on the streets here, as brands from BYD to Changan made aggressive inroads in a market once dominated by South Korea’s Hyundai and Kia, said the driver who picked me up from the airport in a gleaming Changan electric vehicle.
But it was not the rise of Chinese tech that had brought me to this energy-rich pocket of Central Asia; it was an American giant.
